chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Sicilia. An Antechamber in Leontes’ Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Camillo and Archidamus.]
ARCHIDAMUS. Camillo, if you ever visit Bohemia on the kind of errand that brings me here now, you'll see, as I've said, a great difference between our Bohemia and your Sicilia.
CAMILLO. I think this coming summer the King of Sicilia means to pay King Polixenes of Bohemia the visit he rightly owes him.
ARCHIDAMUS. Then our hospitality will shame us. We can only ask to be excused because our love is sincere. For truly —
CAMILLO. Please —

ARCHIDAMUS. Honestly, I'm saying this from what I know. We can't do it with such splendor — in so rare a way — I don't know what to say. We'll give you sleeping drinks, so that your senses, not noticing how little we offer, may not be able to praise us, but will at least blame us less.
CAMILLO. You're paying far too much for what is given freely.
ARCHIDAMUS. Believe me, I speak as my understanding tells me and as my honesty lets me say it.

CAMILLO. The King of Sicilia can't be too kind to Bohemia. They were brought up together as children, and a deep affection took root between them then, which can't help but branch out now. Since their grown-up rank and royal duties separated them, they have met through representatives instead of in person, with exchanges of gifts, letters and loving embassies. So they have seemed to be together though apart. They have shaken hands across a vast distance and embraced from the ends of opposite winds. May heaven keep their love going!

ARCHIDAMUS. I think there is nothing in the world, neither ill will nor any cause, that could change it. You have unspeakable comfort in your young Prince Mamillius. He is a boy of the greatest promise I have ever noticed.

CAMILLO. I quite agree with you about the hopes he raises. He is a gallant child, one who works like medicine on the people and makes old hearts fresh. Those who went on crutches before he was born still want to live to see him a man.
ARCHIDAMUS. Would they not be content to die otherwise?
CAMILLO. Yes, if they had no other excuse for wanting to live.
ARCHIDAMUS. If the king had no son, they would want to live on crutches until he had one.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — The same. A Room of State in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Leontes, Polixenes, Hermione, Mamillius, Camillo and Attendants.]

POLIXENES. Nine times the moon has changed, as the shepherd counts it, since we left our throne unattended. Another nine months would be filled up, my brother, with our thanks, and still we would leave in debt forever. So, like a zero standing in a rich position, I multiply the thousands of thanks already given with one more "we thank you."
LEONTES. Hold your thanks a while, and pay them when you leave.

POLIXENES. Sir, that's tomorrow. My fears question me about what may happen or grow up while we're away. I pray no biting winds blow at home, so we won't have to say, "This worry was too true." Besides, I've stayed long enough to tire your royal self.
LEONTES. We're tougher, brother, than you can wear out.
POLIXENES. I can't stay any longer.
LEONTES. One week longer.
POLIXENES. Truly, tomorrow.
LEONTES. We'll split the time between us, then. In that I'll take no refusal.

POLIXENES. Don't press me, please. No tongue in the whole world could win me as quickly as yours would. It would win me now, if your request were truly necessary, even if I had to refuse it. My affairs drag me homeward. To block that would be, out of your love, a whip to me, and my staying would be a burden and trouble to you. To save us both from that, farewell, our brother.
LEONTES. Tongue-tied, our queen? Speak, you.

HERMIONE. I had thought, sir, to keep silent until you had drawn oaths from him not to stay. You charge him too coldly. Tell him you are sure all is well in Bohemia, since yesterday's news proved it. Say this to him, and he's driven from his best defense.
LEONTES. Well said, Hermione.

HERMIONE. To say he longs to see his son would be a strong reason. But let him say so, then, and let him go. If he swears so, though, he shall not stay. We'll beat him out of here with spinning staffs.
[_To Polixenes._] Yet from your royal presence I'll venture

to borrow a week. When you have my husband visiting you in Bohemia, I'll give him my permission to stay a month beyond the date set for his leaving. And yet, Leontes, truly, I love you not one tick of the clock less than any lady loves her lord. You'll stay?
POLIXENES. No, madam.
HERMIONE. No, but you will?
POLIXENES. I may not, truly.

HERMIONE. "Truly"! You put me off with limp vows. But even if you tried to knock the stars out of their spheres with oaths, I would still say, "Sir, no going." Truly, you shall not go. A lady's "truly" is as powerful as a lord's. Will you go still? Then you force me to keep you as a prisoner, not a guest, and you'll pay your fees when you leave and save your thanks. What do you say? My prisoner or my guest? By your dreaded "truly," you shall be one of them.
POLIXENES. Your guest, then, madam. To be your prisoner would imply an offense, which I'm less able to commit than you are to punish.
HERMIONE. Not your jailer then, but your kind hostess. Come, I'll question you about my lord's tricks and yours when you were boys. You were pretty little lords then.
POLIXENES. We were, fair queen, two lads who thought there was nothing ahead but a tomorrow like today, and being boys forever.
HERMIONE. Wasn't my lord the greater rascal of the two?

POLIXENES. We were like twin lambs frisking in the sun and bleating at each other. What we exchanged was innocence for innocence. We knew nothing of the doctrine of doing wrong, and never dreamed that anyone did. If we had gone on living that life, and our weak spirits had never been raised higher by stronger blood, we could have answered heaven boldly, "Not guilty," with the penalty we inherit wiped clean.
HERMIONE. From this we gather you have tripped since.
POLIXENES. Oh, my most sacred lady, temptations have been born to us since then! In those unfledged days my wife was a girl, and you yourself had not yet crossed the eyes of my young playfellow.

HERMIONE. Heaven help us! Don't conclude anything from this, or you'll say your queen and I are devils. But go on. We'll answer for the offenses we've made you commit, if you sinned with us first, and kept on sinning with us, and slipped with no one but us.
LEONTES. Is he won yet?
HERMIONE. He'll stay, my lord.
LEONTES. At my request he would not. Hermione, my dearest, you never spoke to better purpose.
HERMIONE. Never?
LEONTES. Never but once.

HERMIONE. What! Have I twice said well? When was the first time? Please tell me. Cram us with praise and make us as fat as tame things. One good deed dying unspoken slaughters a thousand waiting on it. Our praises are our wages. You can ride us a thousand furlongs with one soft kiss, before we'd cover an acre when heated by the spur. But to the goal. My last good deed was to ask him to stay. What was my first? It has an elder sister, or I misunderstand you. Oh, I wish her name were Grace! But once before I spoke to the purpose. When? No, let me have it; I long to know.
LEONTES. Why, that was when three bitter months had soured themselves to death, before I could make you open your white hand and clap it in mine as my love. Then you said, "I am yours forever."
HERMIONE. It's Grace indeed. Why, look now, I've spoken to the purpose twice. The one earned a royal husband forever. The other, a friend for a while.
[Giving her hand to Polixenes.]
LEONTES.
[Aside.] Too hot, too hot!

Friendship carried too far is a mixing of bloods. I have _tremor cordis_ on me: my heart is trembling. It dances, but not for joy — not joy. This entertainment may put on a free face, taking its freedom from warmth, from generosity, from an overflowing heart, and it may suit the host well. It may, I grant. But to be paddling palms and pinching fingers, as they are now, and making practiced smiles as in a looking-glass, and then to sigh, like the horn blown when a deer is killed — oh, that is entertainment my heart doesn't like, nor my brow. Mamillius, are you my boy?
MAMILLIUS. Ay, my good lord.

LEONTES. By my faith! Why, that's my fine fellow. What! Have you smudged your nose? They say it's a copy of mine. Come, captain, we must be neat. Not neat, but clean, captain. And yet the steer, the heifer and the calf are all called neat, meaning horned cattle. — Is she still fingering his palm, like someone playing a keyboard? — How now, you wanton calf! Are you my calf?
MAMILLIUS. Yes, if you like, my lord.

LEONTES. You lack a rough head and the budding horns that I have, to be fully like me. Yet they say we are almost as alike as eggs. Women say so, and women will say anything. But even if they were as false as over-dyed black cloth, as wind, as waters, as false as loaded dice to a man who draws no boundary between what's his and what's mine, it would still be true to say this boy is like me. Come, sir page, look at me with your sky-blue eye. Sweet rascal! Dearest! My piece of flesh! Can your mother — ? May it be? Affection! Your force stabs to the center. You make possible what was thought impossible, and you share things with dreams. How can this be? You are partner with what's unreal and companion to nothing, so it's quite believable that you can join with something. And you do, beyond all bounds, and I find it so, to the infection of my brain and the hardening of my brow.
POLIXENES. What does Sicilia mean by that?
HERMIONE. He seems somewhat unsettled.
POLIXENES. How, my lord? How are you? How is it with you, best brother?
HERMIONE. You look as if you wore a very distracted brow. Are you moved, my lord?

LEONTES. No, truly. How sometimes nature betrays its folly and its tenderness, and makes itself a plaything for harder hearts! Looking at the lines of my boy's face, I thought I recoiled twenty-three years and saw myself unbreeched, in my green velvet coat, with my dagger muzzled so it wouldn't bite its master and prove, as ornaments often do, too dangerous. How like this kernel, this squash of an unripe pea, this gentleman, I thought I was then. My honest friend, will you take eggs for money?
MAMILLIUS. No, my lord, I'll fight.
LEONTES. You will? Why, good luck to you! My brother, are you as fond of your young prince as we seem to be of ours?

POLIXENES. At home, sir, he's all my exercise, my mirth, my business. Now my sworn friend, and then my enemy. My parasite, my soldier, my statesman, everything. He makes a July day as short as December, and with his changing childishness he cures thoughts in me that would thicken my blood.

LEONTES. This little squire holds the same office with me. We two will walk, my lord, and leave you to your graver steps. Hermione, show how you love us in welcoming our brother. Let what is dear in Sicilia be cheap. Next to yourself and my young rover, he's closest to my heart.
HERMIONE. If you want to find us, we're yours in the garden. Shall we attend you there?

LEONTES. Do as you please. You'll be found, so long as you're under the sky. [_Aside._] I'm angling now, though you don't see how I let out line. Go on, go on! How she holds up her beak, her bill, to him! And arms herself with a wife's boldness toward her permitting husband!
[Exeunt Polixenes, Hermione and Attendants.]

Gone already! Inch-thick, knee-deep, over head and ears — a forked one, a man with horns! — Go, play, boy, play. Your mother plays, and I play too, but in such a disgraced part, whose outcome will hiss me to my grave. Contempt and clamor will be my funeral bell. Go, play, boy, play. There have been cuckolds before now, or I'm much deceived. And there are many men even now, while I say this, holding their wives by the arm, who little think she has been flooded in his absence and his pond fished by his next neighbor — by Sir Smile, his neighbor. No, there's comfort in it. Other men have gates, and those gates are opened, as mine is, against their will. If all who have unfaithful wives despaired, a tenth of mankind would hang themselves. There's no cure for it. It's a bawdy planet that strikes wherever it rules, and it's powerful, believe it, from east, west, north and south. Let it be concluded: there's no barricade for a belly. Know it: it lets the enemy in and out with bag and baggage. Many thousands of us have the disease and don't feel it. — How now, boy!
MAMILLIUS. I am like you, they say.
LEONTES. Why, that's some comfort. What! Camillo there?
CAMILLO. Ay, my good lord.
LEONTES. Go play, Mamillius; you're an honest man.
[Exit Mamillius.]
Camillo, this great sir will stay longer yet.
CAMILLO. You had a hard time making his anchor hold. When you cast it out, it kept coming home.
LEONTES. Did you notice it?
CAMILLO. He would not stay at your petitions. He made his business more pressing.
LEONTES. Did you perceive it?
[_Aside._] They're here with me already, whispering and murmuring in ears,
"Sicilia is a so-and-so." It has gone far by the time I'm the last to taste it. — How did it come about, Camillo, that he stayed?
CAMILLO. At the good queen's request.

LEONTES. At the queen's request, so be it. The word "good" should fit there, but as things are, it doesn't. Was this noticed by any mind but yours? For your wit is absorbent and draws in more than common blockheads. It wasn't noticed, was it, except by the finer natures? By a few of extraordinary brains? Lower tables, perhaps, are blind to this business. Say.
CAMILLO. Business, my lord? I think most people understand that Bohemia is staying here longer.
LEONTES. Ha?
CAMILLO. Staying here longer.
LEONTES. Ay, but why?
CAMILLO. To satisfy your highness, and the requests of our most gracious mistress.

LEONTES. Satisfy? The requests of your mistress? Satisfy? Let that be enough. I have trusted you, Camillo, with everything nearest my heart, including my private counsels, in which, like a priest, you cleansed my heart. I left you a reformed penitent. But we have been deceived in your integrity, deceived in what seems so.
CAMILLO. Heaven forbid, my lord!

LEONTES. I'll stand by it: you are not honest. Or, if you lean that way, you are a coward, who hamstrings honesty from behind and holds it back from the course it requires. Or else you must be counted a servant grafted into my serious trust, and negligent in it. Or else a fool, who sees a game played to the end, the rich stake drawn, and takes it all for a joke.

CAMILLO. My gracious lord, I may be negligent, foolish and fearful. No man is free of all of these. His negligence, folly or fear shows itself at some time among the infinite doings of the world. In your affairs, my lord, if I was ever willfully negligent, it was my folly. If I deliberately played the fool, it was my negligence, not weighing the end well. If I was ever afraid to do something when I doubted the outcome, and the doing of it cried out against leaving it undone, it was a fear that often affects the wisest. These, my lord, are such allowed weaknesses that honesty is never free of them. But I beg Your Grace, be plainer with me. Let me know my offense by its own face. If I then deny it, it's none of mine.

LEONTES. Haven't you seen, Camillo? (But that's beyond doubt: you have, or your eye's lens is thicker than a cuckold's horn.) Or heard? (For a sight so obvious, rumor can't be silent.) Or thought? (For thinking doesn't live in a man who doesn't think.) That my wife is slippery? If you will confess it, or else shamelessly deny it, with no eyes, no ears, no thought, then say my wife's a hobby-horse, a loose woman, who deserves a name as foul as any flax-wench who goes to bed before her betrothal. Say it and justify it.

CAMILLO. I would not stand by and hear my sovereign mistress slandered without taking vengeance on the spot. Curse my heart, you never said anything that suited you less than this. To repeat it would be as deep a sin as saying it, even if it were true.

LEONTES. Is whispering nothing? Is leaning cheek to cheek? Is touching noses? Kissing with the inside of the lip? Stopping the course of laughter with a sigh — an infallible sign of breaking honesty? Mounting foot on foot? Skulking in corners? Wishing clocks faster, hours into minutes, noon into midnight? And all eyes blind with cataracts but theirs, theirs only, who would be wicked unseen? Is this nothing? Why, then the world and everything in it is nothing, the covering sky is nothing, Bohemia is nothing, my wife is nothing, and these nothings have nothing, if this is nothing.
CAMILLO. My good lord, be cured of this diseased opinion, and soon, for it is most dangerous.
LEONTES. Say it is. It's true.
CAMILLO. No, no, my lord.

LEONTES. It is. You lie, you lie. I say you lie, Camillo, and I hate you. I pronounce you a gross lout, a mindless slave, or else a hovering fence-sitter who can see good and evil at once with your eyes and lean toward both. If my wife's liver were as infected as her life, she wouldn't live the running of one hourglass.
CAMILLO. Who infects her?

LEONTES. Why, he who wears her like a medal hanging about his neck: Bohemia. If I had true servants around me, who had eyes to see my honor as they see their own profits, they would do what would put an end to further wrongdoing. Yes, and you, his cupbearer — whom I raised from a lower rank and seated in honor, who can see as plainly as heaven sees earth and earth sees heaven how I am galled — you might spice a cup to give my enemy a lasting sleep. That drink would be a cordial to me.

CAMILLO. Sir, my lord, I could do this, and with no rash potion, but with a lingering dose that would not work maliciously like poison. But I can't believe this crack is in my dread mistress, who is so supremely honorable. I have loved you —

LEONTES. Go ahead and doubt it, then, and go rot! Do you think I'm so muddy, so unsettled, as to set myself up for this torment? To stain the purity and whiteness of my sheets (which, kept clean, mean sleep, and spotted, mean goads, thorns, nettles and wasps' tails)? To give scandal to the blood of the prince my son (whom I think mine, and love as mine), without a ripe reason? Would I do this? Could a man so flinch?

CAMILLO. I must believe you, sir. I do, and I will remove Bohemia for you. But on this condition: when he's gone, your highness must take your queen back as yours at first, for your son's sake, and so seal up the injury of tongues in courts and kingdoms known and allied to yours.
LEONTES. You advise me exactly as I have set my own course. I'll put no blemish on her honor, none.

CAMILLO. My lord, go then, and with a face as clear as friendship wears at feasts, stay with Bohemia and with your queen. I am his cupbearer. If he gets a wholesome drink from me, don't count me your servant.
LEONTES. This is all: do it, and you have half my heart. Don't, and you split your own.
CAMILLO. I'll do it, my lord.
LEONTES. I will seem friendly, as you've advised me.
[Exit.]

CAMILLO. Oh, miserable lady! But as for me, what a position I'm in! I must be the poisoner of good Polixenes, and my reason for doing it is obedience to a master who, in rebellion against himself, wants everyone who is his to rebel too. Promotion follows this deed. If I could find an example of thousands who struck anointed kings and prospered after, I would not do it. But since neither brass, nor stone, nor parchment records even one, let villainy itself reject it. I must leave the court. Whether I do it or not, it's certain ruin for me. Let a lucky star rule now! Here comes Bohemia.
[Enter Polixenes.]
POLIXENES. This is strange. I think my favor here is beginning to warp. Not speak? Good day, Camillo.
CAMILLO. Hail, most royal sir!
POLIXENES. What's the news in court?
CAMILLO. None rare, my lord.

POLIXENES. The king has such a look on him as if he had lost a province, a region loved as he loves himself. Just now I met him with the usual courtesy, and he turned his eyes the other way, let fall a lip of great contempt, and hurried from me. So he leaves me to wonder what is brewing that changes his manners like this.
CAMILLO. I dare not know, my lord.

POLIXENES. How, dare not? Do not? Do you know and dare not? Make it clear to me. It's something like that. For what you know, you must know yourself, and you cannot say you dare not. Good Camillo, your changed looks are a mirror to me that shows me mine changed too. For I must be a party in this alteration, finding myself so altered with it.
CAMILLO. There is a sickness that puts some of us in disorder, but I cannot name the disease, and it is caught from you, who are yet well.

POLIXENES. How, caught from me? Don't make me out to have the eyes of a basilisk. I have looked on thousands who did better for my regard, but killed none so. Camillo — as you are certainly a gentleman, and what's more learned like a clerk and experienced, which adorns our gentry no less than our parents' noble names, by whose success we are gentle — I beg you, if you know anything it's right for me to be informed of, don't imprison it in concealment that keeps me ignorant.
CAMILLO. I may not answer.

POLIXENES. A sickness caught from me, and yet I'm well? I must have an answer. Do you hear, Camillo? I conjure you by all the parts of manhood that honor acknowledges, of which the least is this request of mine, that you declare what harm you guess is creeping toward me: how far off, how near, which way it can be prevented if it can, and if not, how best to bear it.

CAMILLO. Sir, I will tell you, since I'm charged in honor, and by one I think honorable. So mark my advice, which must be followed as swiftly as I mean to say it, or both you and I will cry "lost," and so good night!
POLIXENES. On, good Camillo.
CAMILLO. I am appointed to murder you.
POLIXENES. By whom, Camillo?
CAMILLO. By the king.
POLIXENES. For what?
CAMILLO. He thinks, no, he swears with all confidence, as if he had seen it, or had himself been the tool that drove you to it, that you have touched his queen in a forbidden way.

POLIXENES. Oh, then may my best blood turn to infected jelly, and my name be yoked with the name of Judas, who betrayed the Best! Turn my freshest reputation into a stink that strikes the dullest nose wherever I arrive, and let my approach be shunned, no, hated, worse than the greatest plague ever heard or read of!

CAMILLO. Swear against his thought by every star in heaven and all their influences, and you might as well forbid the sea to obey the moon. You can't remove or shake by oath or advice the structure of his folly, whose foundation is piled on his faith and will last as long as his body stands.
POLIXENES. How should this grow?

CAMILLO. I don't know. But I am sure it's safer to avoid what has grown than to ask how it was born. So, if you dare trust my honesty, which lies enclosed in this body of mine, which you can take along as a pledge, then leave tonight. I will whisper your followers into the business and clear them out of the city by twos and threes at different back gates. As for myself, I'll put my fortunes at your service, which are lost here by this discovery. Don't be uncertain, for by the honor of my parents I have told the truth. If you seek to prove it, I dare not stand by, nor will you be any safer than one condemned by the king's own mouth, with his execution sworn.

POLIXENES. I believe you. I saw his heart in his face. Give me your hand. Be my pilot, and your place shall always be next to mine. My ships are ready, and my people expected my departure two days ago. This jealousy is for a precious creature. As she is rare, it must be great. As his person is mighty, it must be violent. And since he thinks he is dishonored by a man who always professed friendship to him, his revenges must be made all the more bitter. Fear overshadows me. May good speed be my friend, and comfort the gracious queen, part of his theme but nothing to do with his ill-taken suspicion! Come, Camillo, I will respect you as a father if you carry my life safely away from here. Let us go.
CAMILLO. It is in my authority to command the keys of all the back gates. Please your highness, take the urgent hour. Come, sir, away.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Sicilia. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Hermione, Mamillius and Ladies.]
HERMIONE. Take the boy away. He troubles me so, it's past enduring.
FIRST LADY. Come, my gracious lord, shall I be your playfellow?
MAMILLIUS. No, I'll have none of you.
FIRST LADY. Why, my sweet lord?
MAMILLIUS. You'll kiss me hard and talk to me as if I were still a baby. I like you better.
SECOND LADY. And why so, my lord?
MAMILLIUS. Not because your brows are blacker. Though black brows, they say, suit some women best, as long as there isn't too much hair there, but it's in a semicircle or a half-moon made with a pen.
SECOND LADY. Who taught you this?
MAMILLIUS. I learned it from women's faces. Now tell me, what color are your eyebrows?
FIRST LADY. Blue, my lord.
MAMILLIUS. No, that's a joke. I have seen a lady's nose that was blue, but not her eyebrows.
FIRST LADY. Listen, your mother the queen is getting round fast. One of these days we'll be offering our services to a fine new prince, and then you'd play with us, if we'd let you.
SECOND LADY. She has grown lately into a goodly size. May good time meet her!
HERMIONE. What wisdom is stirring among you? Come, sir, now I'm for you again. Please sit by us and tell us a tale.
MAMILLIUS. Shall it be merry or sad?
HERMIONE. As merry as you like.
MAMILLIUS. A sad tale is best for winter. I have one of sprites and goblins.
HERMIONE. Let's have that, good sir. Come on, sit down. Come on, and do your best to frighten me with your sprites. You're powerful at it.
MAMILLIUS. There was a man —
HERMIONE. No, come, sit down, then go on.
MAMILLIUS. Dwelt by a churchyard. I will tell it softly. Those crickets over there shall not hear it.
HERMIONE. Come on then, and give it to me in my ear.
[Enter Leontes, Antigonus, Lords and Guards.]
LEONTES. Was he seen there? His attendants? Camillo with him?
FIRST LORD. Behind the clump of pines I met them. I never saw men hurry so on their way. I watched them right to their ships.

LEONTES. How blessed I am in my just judgment, in my true opinion! Alas, for lesser knowledge! How cursed in being so blessed! There may be a spider steeped in the cup, and one may drink and leave and take in no venom, since his knowledge is not infected. But if someone shows the hated ingredient to his eye and makes known how he has drunk, he cracks his throat and sides with violent heaves. I have drunk, and seen the spider. Camillo was his helper in this, his pander. There is a plot against my life and my crown. All that I suspected is true. That false villain whom I employed was already employed by him. He has discovered my plan, and I remain a pinched thing, yes, a very trick for them to play with at will. How did the back gates come to be so easily open?
FIRST LORD. By his great authority, which has often prevailed no less than that over your command.
LEONTES. I know it too well. Give me the boy. I am glad you did not nurse him. Though he bears some signs of me, you have too much of your blood in him.
HERMIONE. What is this? A game?
LEONTES. Take the boy away. He shall not come near her. Away with him, and let her amuse herself with what she's pregnant with, for it's Polixenes who has made you swell this way.
[Exit Mamillius with some of the Guards.]
HERMIONE. But I'd say he did not, and I'll be sworn you would believe my saying, however you hear it denied.

LEONTES. You, my lords, look at her, mark her well. Be about to say "she is a goodly lady," and the justice of your hearts will add "It's a pity she's not honest, honorable." Praise her only for this outward form of hers, which on my faith deserves high speech, and straight away the shrug, the hum or ha, these petty brands that slander uses — oh, I'm wrong, it is mercy that uses them, since slander would sear even virtue itself — these shrugs, these hums and has, when you have said "she's goodly," come between before you can say "she's honest." But let it be known, from him who has most cause to grieve that it should be so, she's an adulteress!
HERMIONE. Should a villain say so, the most overflowing villain in the world, he'd be that much more a villain. You, my lord, are only mistaken.

LEONTES. You have mistaken, my lady, Polixenes for Leontes. Oh, you thing, whom I won't call a creature of your rank, lest barbarism, making me the precedent, should use like language to all ranks and leave out mannerly distinction between prince and beggar. I have said she's an adulteress. I have said with whom. More, she's a traitor, and Camillo is an accomplice with her, and one who knows what she should be ashamed to know herself except with her most vile principal: that she's a bed-swerver, as bad as those whom the common people give boldest names. Yes, and privy to this their late escape.

HERMIONE. No, by my life, privy to none of this. How this will grieve you when you come to clearer knowledge, that you have so proclaimed me! Gentle my lord, you can scarcely right me thoroughly then, by saying you were mistaken.

LEONTES. No. If I mistake in those foundations I build on, the earth's center isn't big enough to bear a schoolboy's top. Away with her to prison! He who speaks for her is guilty at a distance, merely by speaking.

HERMIONE. Some ill planet reigns. I must be patient until the heavens look with a more favorable aspect. Good my lords, I am not prone to weeping, as our sex commonly is. The lack of this vain dew may perhaps dry up your pity. But I have an honorable grief lodged here that burns worse than tears drown. I beg you all, my lords, to judge me with thoughts as kindly as your charity best instructs you. And so let the king's will be done.
LEONTES. Shall I be heard?

HERMIONE. Who goes with me? Please, your highness, let my women be with me, for you see my condition requires it. Don't weep, good fools. There is no cause. When you know your mistress has deserved prison, then abound in tears as I come out. This action I now go on is for my better grace. Goodbye, my lord. I never wished to see you sorry. Now I trust I shall. My women, come; you have leave.
LEONTES. Go, do as we bid. Out!
[Exeunt Queen and Ladies with Guards.]
FIRST LORD. I beg your highness, call the queen back.
ANTIGONUS. Be certain what you do, sir, lest your justice prove violence, in which three great ones suffer: yourself, your queen, your son.

FIRST LORD. For her, my lord, I dare lay down my life, and will do it, sir, if you please to accept it, that the queen is spotless in the eyes of heaven and in yours — I mean in this matter of which you accuse her.

ANTIGONUS. If it proves she's otherwise, I'll keep my stables where I lodge my wife. I'll go in couples with her. I won't trust her any further than I can feel and see her. For every inch of woman in the world, every dram of woman's flesh, is false, if she is.
LEONTES. Hold your peace.
FIRST LORD. Good my lord —

ANTIGONUS. It is for you we speak, not for ourselves. You are abused, and by some instigator who will be damned for it. I wish I knew the villain. I would damn him thoroughly. If she is flawed in honor, I have three daughters. The eldest is eleven, the second and third are nine and about five. If this proves true, they'll pay for it. By my honor, I'll geld them all. They shall not see fourteen, to bring forth false generations. They are co-heirs, and I would rather castrate myself than have them not produce fair issue.
LEONTES. Stop; no more. You smell this business with a sense as cold as a dead man's nose. But I see it and feel it, as you feel when I do this, and I see besides the instruments that feel.
ANTIGONUS. If it is so, we need no grave to bury honesty. There's not a grain of it to sweeten the face of the whole dungy earth.
LEONTES. What! Am I not believed?
FIRST LORD. I'd rather you were the one not believed than I, my lord, on this ground. And it would content me more to have her honor true than your suspicion, however I'm blamed for it.

LEONTES. Why, what need have we to discuss this with you, rather than follow our forceful instinct? Our prerogative doesn't call for your counsels. Our natural goodness imparts this. If you, whether dulled or seeming so in skill, cannot or will not relish a truth, then inform yourselves, as we have, that we need no more of your advice. The matter, the loss, the gain, the ordering of it, is all properly ours.
ANTIGONUS. And I wish, my liege, you had tried it only in your silent judgment, without more opening of it.

LEONTES. How could that be? Either you are most ignorant by age, or you were born a fool. Camillo's flight, added to their familiarity, pushes this proceeding on. Their familiarity was as gross as ever touched on guesswork, lacking only sight, with nothing needed for proof but seeing, all other circumstances making up the deed. Yet, for greater confirmation (for in an act of this importance it would be most pitiful to be wild), I have dispatched in haste to sacred Delphos, to Apollo's temple, Cleomenes and Dion, whom you know to be men of ample ability. Now from the oracle they will bring everything, and its spiritual counsel, once had, shall stop or spur me. Have I done well?
FIRST LORD. Well done, my lord.

LEONTES. Though I am satisfied and need no more than what I know, the oracle shall still give rest to the minds of others, such as the man whose ignorant credulity will not rise to the truth. So we have thought it good that she be confined away from our free person, lest the treachery of the two who fled be left for her to carry out. Come, follow us. We are to speak in public, for this business will get us all stirred up.
ANTIGONUS.
[Aside.] To laughter, I take it,
if the good truth were known.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 2 — The same. The outer Room of a Prison
paragraphs: [Enter Paulina, a Gentleman and Attendants.]
PAULINA. Call the keeper of the prison. Let him know who I am.
[Exit the Gentleman.]
Good lady! No court in Europe is too good for you. What are you doing in a prison?
[Enter Gentleman with the Gaoler.]
Now, good sir, you know me, don't you?
GAOLER. Yes, madam, you're a worthy lady, and one I greatly respect.
PAULINA. Then please take me to the queen.
GAOLER. I can't, madam. I have a direct order against it.
PAULINA. What a fuss, to lock honesty and honor away from gentle visitors! Is it lawful, please, to see her women? Any of them? Emilia?
GAOLER. If you'll send these attendants of yours aside, madam, I'll bring Emilia out.
PAULINA. Please, then, call her. You all, step back.
[Exeunt Gentleman and Attendants.]
GAOLER. And, madam, I must be present at your conversation.
PAULINA. Well, so be it, please.
[Exit Gaoler.]
What a fuss, to make a stain out of something that has no stain, beyond any coloring-over.
[Re-enter Gaoler with Emilia.]
Dear gentlewoman, how is our gracious lady?

EMILIA. As well as someone so great and so forsaken can hold together. After her frights and griefs, which no tender lady ever bore worse, she has gone into labor and has given birth, somewhat before her time.
PAULINA. A boy?
EMILIA. A daughter, and a fine baby, strong and likely to live. The queen takes great comfort in her, and says, "My poor prisoner, I am as innocent as you."

PAULINA. I'd swear to it. These dangerous, unsafe fits in the king, curse them! He must be told about this, and he shall be. The job suits a woman best. I'll take it on myself. If I turn out sweet-mouthed, let my tongue blister, and may I never again be the trumpet of my red-faced anger. Please, Emilia, give the queen my best respects. If she dares trust me with her little baby, I'll show her to the king, and I'll promise to be the queen's advocate at the top of my voice. We don't know how he may soften at the sight of the child. The silence of pure innocence often persuades when speaking fails.

EMILIA. Most worthy madam, your honor and your goodness are so plain that your generous offer can't fail to succeed. There is no lady living so fit for this great errand. Please, madam, go into the next room. I'll tell the queen of your noble offer right away. She was only just now turning over this very plan, but she didn't dare ask an honorable person to do it, for fear of being refused.
PAULINA. Tell her, Emilia, that I'll use the tongue I have. If wit flows from it as boldly as courage flows from my heart, there's no doubt I'll do some good.
EMILIA. Now bless you for it! I'll go to the queen. Please come a little nearer.
GAOLER. Madam, if the queen is pleased to send the baby, I don't know what trouble I'll bring on myself by letting her through, since I have no warrant.

PAULINA. You needn't fear it, sir. This child was a prisoner in the womb, and by the law and course of great nature she has been set free from there. She has no part in the king's anger, and no guilt in the queen's offense, if there is any.
GAOLER. I do believe it.
PAULINA. Don't be afraid. On my honor, I will stand between you and any danger.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 3 — The same. A Room in the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Leontes, Antigonus, Lords and other Attendants.]

LEONTES. No rest by night or day. It's only weakness to bear this matter like this, mere weakness. If the cause didn't exist (part of the cause, I mean, is she, the adulteress, because the whore's king, Polixenes, is far beyond my reach, out of the range and aim of my brain, plot-proof). But her I can hook to me. Say she were gone, given to the fire. Half my peace of mind might come back to me. Who's there?
FIRST ATTENDANT. My lord.
LEONTES. How is the boy?
FIRST ATTENDANT. He slept well tonight. It's hoped his sickness is gone.

LEONTES. To see his nobleness, understanding the dishonor of his mother! He drooped at once, took it deeply to heart, fastened and fixed the shame of it in himself, threw off his spirit, his appetite, his sleep, and simply wasted away. Leave me alone. Go, see how he is.
[Exit First Attendant.]

Enough, enough! Don't think of him. The very thought of taking my revenge that way rebounds on me. Polixenes is too mighty in himself, and in his allies and his alliances. Let him be, until a time may serve. For revenge now, take it on her. Camillo and Polixenes laugh at me and make a pastime of my sorrow. They wouldn't laugh if I could reach them, and neither will she, while she is in my power.
[Enter Paulina carrying a baby, with Antigonus, lords and servants.]
FIRST LORD. You must not go in.

PAULINA. No, rather, good my lords, stand with me. Do you fear his tyrannous passion more than the queen's life, alas? She is a gracious, innocent soul, more free of guilt than he is full of jealousy.
ANTIGONUS. That's enough.
SERVANT. Madam, he hasn't slept tonight. He has commanded that no one come near him.

PAULINA. Not so hot, good sir. I come to bring him sleep. It's people like you, who creep around him like shadows and sigh at each of his needless heaves, who feed the cause of his sleeplessness. I come with words as healing as they are true, as honest as either, to purge him of the mood that keeps him from sleep.
LEONTES. What noise is that out there, ho?
PAULINA. No noise, my lord, but needed conversation about some godparents for your highness.
LEONTES. What! Away with that audacious woman! Antigonus, I ordered you to keep her from coming near me. I knew she would.
ANTIGONUS. I told her so, my lord, on peril of your displeasure and of mine, that she must not visit you.
LEONTES. What, can't you control her?
PAULINA. He can control me away from anything dishonest. In this, unless he takes the course you have taken and puts me in prison for doing right, believe it, he will not control me.
ANTIGONUS. There now, you hear her. When she takes the reins I let her run, but she won't stumble.

PAULINA. Good my liege, I come, and I beg you to hear me. I profess myself your loyal servant, your physician, your most obedient counselor. Yet I dare show it less, in comforting your sufferings, than those who seem most to be yours. I say I come from your good queen.
LEONTES. Good queen!
PAULINA. Good queen, my lord, good queen. I say, good queen. If I were a man, even the worst man around you, I would prove her good by combat.
LEONTES. Force her out.

PAULINA. Let anyone who makes so little of his eyes lay hands on me first. I'll go of my own accord. But first I'll do my errand. The good queen (for she is good) has brought you a daughter. Here she is. The queen commends her to your blessing.
[Laying down the child.]
LEONTES. Out! A mannish witch! Out the door with her! A most spying bawd!
PAULINA. Not so. I know as little about that as you do, in giving me that title, and I am no less honest than you are mad, which is enough, I'll guarantee, as this world goes, to pass for honest.

LEONTES. Traitors! Will you not push her out? [_To Antigonus._] Give her the bastard, you dotard! You're henpecked, driven out of your own roost by your Dame Partlet here. Take up the bastard, take it up, I say. Give it to your old crone.
PAULINA. May your hands be forever unworthy of respect if you pick up the princess under that forced disgrace of bastardy which he has put upon her!
LEONTES. He's afraid of his wife.
PAULINA. I wish you were. Then it would be beyond all doubt that you'd call your children yours.
LEONTES. A nest of traitors!
ANTIGONUS. I am none, by this good light.

PAULINA. Nor I. Nor is anyone here, except one, and that's himself. For he betrays his own sacred honor, his queen's, his hopeful son's and his baby's, to slander, whose sting is sharper than the sword's. And he will not (for, as the case now stands, it is a curse he cannot be forced to) pull up the root of his opinion, which is as rotten as ever oak or stone was sound.

LEONTES. A scold of boundless tongue, who recently beat her husband, and now harasses me! This brat is none of mine. It is the offspring of Polixenes. Out with it, and together with its mother, put them both to the fire.

PAULINA. It is yours. And, if we might lay the old proverb to your charge, she is so like you, it's the worse for her. Look, my lords, although the print is small, she is the whole matter and copy of her father: eye, nose, lip, the trick of his frown, his forehead. Yes, the valley, the pretty dimples of his chin and cheek, his smiles, the very mold and frame of hand, nail and finger. And you, good goddess Nature, who have made her so like him that fathered her, if you have the ordering of her mind too, among all colors let there be no yellow in it, lest she suspect, as he does, that her children are not her husband's!
LEONTES. A gross hag! And you, you good-for-nothing, you deserve to be hanged for not stopping her tongue.
ANTIGONUS. Hang all the husbands who can't do that feat, and you'll hardly be left with one subject.
LEONTES. Once more, take her away.
PAULINA. A most unworthy and unnatural lord can do no more.
LEONTES. I'll have you burned.

PAULINA. I don't care. It is the heretic who makes the fire, not the one who burns in it. I won't call you tyrant. But this most cruel treatment of your queen, unable to produce any accusation beyond your own weak-hinged fancy, smacks somewhat of tyranny, and will make you ignoble, yes, a scandal to the world.
LEONTES. On your allegiance, out of the room with her! If I were a tyrant, where would her life be? She wouldn't dare call me so, if she knew me to be one. Away with her!

PAULINA. Please don't push me. I'll go. Look to your baby, my lord. She's yours. May Jove send her a better guiding spirit! Why do you need these hands? You who are so tender over his follies will never do him any good, not one of you. So, so. Farewell. We are gone.
[Exit.]

LEONTES. You, traitor, have set your wife on to this. My child? Away with it! Even you, who have such a tender heart over it, take it away and see it burned up at once. Even you, and none but you. Take it up right now. Within the hour bring me word it's done, and with good witnesses, or I'll seize your life, along with whatever else you call yours. If you refuse, and want to face my wrath, say so. Then I'll dash the bastard's brains out with my own hands. Go, take it to the fire, for you set your wife on.
ANTIGONUS. I did not, sir. These lords, my noble fellows, if they please, can clear me of it.
LORDS We can. My royal liege, he is not guilty of her coming here.
LEONTES. You're all liars.

FIRST LORD. We beg your highness, give us better credit. We have always served you truly, and we beg you to think of us so. And on our knees we beg, in return for our dear services past and to come, that you change this purpose, which, being so horrible and so bloody, must lead on to some foul result. We all kneel.

LEONTES. I am a feather for every wind that blows. Shall I live on to see this bastard kneel and call me father? Better to burn it now than curse it then. But so be it. Let it live. No, it shall not either. [_To Antigonus._] You, sir, come here, you who have been so tenderly officious with Lady Margery, your midwife there, to save this bastard's life (for it is a bastard, as sure as this beard is gray). What will you risk to save this brat's life?
ANTIGONUS. Anything, my lord, that my ability can undertake and nobleness can impose. At least this much: I'll pledge the little blood I have left to save the innocent. Anything possible.
LEONTES. It shall be possible. Swear by this sword that you will carry out my orders.
ANTIGONUS. I will, my lord.

LEONTES. Mark it, and do it, do you see? Failure in any point of it shall be death not only to you but to your lewd-tongued wife, whom we pardon for this time. We order you, as you are our sworn man, to carry this female bastard away, and to take it to some remote and desert place, quite out of our dominions. There you are to leave it, with no more mercy, to its own protection and the favor of the climate. As it came to us by strange fortune, so I charge you in justice, on peril of your soul and torture of your body, to commit it strangely to some place where chance may nurse it or end it. Take it up.

ANTIGONUS. I swear to do this, though instant death would have been more merciful. Come on, poor baby. May some powerful spirit teach the kites and ravens to be your nurses! Wolves and bears, they say, putting aside their savageness, have done such offices of pity. Sir, may you prosper in more than this deed requires! And may a blessing fight on your side against this cruelty, poor thing, condemned to loss!
[Exit with the child.]
LEONTES. No, I won't raise another man's offspring.
[Enter a Servant.]
SERVANT. Please your highness, messengers from those you sent to the oracle arrived an hour ago. Cleomenes and Dion, having landed safely from Delphos, are both hurrying to the court.
FIRST LORD. If it please you, sir, their speed has been beyond all expectation.

LEONTES. They have been away twenty-three days. That is good speed. It foretells that great Apollo will soon have the truth of this made to appear. Prepare yourselves, lords. Summon a session, so that we may arraign our most disloyal lady. For, as she has been publicly accused, so she shall have a just and open trial. While she lives, my heart will be a burden to me. Leave me, and think on my orders.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Sicilia. A Street in some Town
paragraphs: [Enter Cleomenes and Dion.]
CLEOMENES The climate is delightful, the air very sweet, the island fertile, and the temple far better than the common praise it gets.

DION. I'll report on what struck me most, the heavenly robes (I think that's the right word for them) and the reverence of the solemn men who wore them. Oh, the sacrifice! How ceremonious, solemn and unearthly it was in the offering!
CLEOMENES But above all, the burst and ear-deafening voice of the oracle, like Jove's thunder, so overwhelmed my senses that I felt I was nothing.
DION. If the outcome of this journey turns out as well for the queen (oh, let it be so!) as the journey itself has been for us, rare, pleasant and quick, then the time is well spent.
CLEOMENES Great Apollo, turn everything to the best! These proclamations, which force faults on Hermione, I don't like much.

DION. The violence of the whole business will either clear it up or end it. When the oracle, sealed up by Apollo's great priest, reveals its contents, something rare will come to light even then. Go on. Fresh horses! And may the outcome be gracious!
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same. A Court of Justice
paragraphs: [Enter Leontes, Lords and Officers appear, properly seated.]

LEONTES. This session (we declare it to our great grief) pushes hard against our heart. The person on trial is the daughter of a king, our wife, and one who is too much beloved by us. Let us be cleared of being tyrannous, since we proceed so openly in justice, which shall have its due course, to the end, whether guilt or acquittal. Bring in the prisoner.
OFFICER. It is his highness's pleasure that the queen appear in person here in court. Silence!
[Hermione is brought in guarded; Paulina and Ladies attending.]
LEONTES. Read the indictment.
OFFICER.
[_Reads._] "Hermione, queen to the worthy Leontes, king of Sicilia,

you are here accused and arraigned of high treason, in committing adultery with Polixenes, king of Bohemia, and conspiring with Camillo to take away the life of our sovereign lord the king, your royal husband. The plot being partly laid open by circumstances, you, Hermione, contrary to the faith and allegiance of a true subject, did counsel and aid them, for their better safety, to flee away by night."

HERMIONE. Since what I have to say can only contradict my accusation, and the only testimony on my side is what comes from myself, it will hardly help me to say "Not guilty." My integrity, being counted as falsehood, will be received as falsehood however I express it. But this much I say. If divine powers watch our human actions, as they do, I don't doubt that innocence will make false accusation blush, and tyranny tremble at patience. You, my lord, know best, though you least want to seem to, that my past life has been as continent, as chaste and as true as I am now unhappy. That is more than history can match, even if it were invented and played to catch spectators. For look at me. I am a partner of the royal bed, I own half the throne, I am a great king's daughter and the mother of a promising prince. And here I stand, to chatter and talk for my life and honor in front of whoever pleases to come and hear. As for life, I value it as I value grief, which I would gladly spare myself. As for honor, it passes down from me to my children, and it is the only thing I stand for. I appeal to your own conscience, sir. Before Polixenes came to your court, how I stood in your favor, and how I deserved to. Since he came, what improper conduct I have shown to appear like this. If I went one jot beyond the bound of honor, in act or in wish inclining that way, then let the hearts of all who hear me be hardened, and my nearest kin cry shame on my grave!
LEONTES. I have never yet heard that any of these bolder vices lacked less impudence in denying what they did than in doing it first.
HERMIONE. That's true enough, though it's a saying, sir, that doesn't apply to me.
LEONTES. You will not own it.

HERMIONE. I must not acknowledge at all anything that comes to me in the name of a fault, more than I'm mistress of. As for Polixenes, with whom I am accused, I do confess I loved him as his honor required, with the kind of love that might suit a lady like me. It was love just like that, and no other, as you yourself commanded. Not to have given it, I think, would have been both disobedience and ingratitude, to you and toward your friend, whose love has spoken freely since he could speak, from infancy, to say that it was yours. Now, for conspiracy, I don't know how it tastes, though it has been dished up for me to find out. All I know of it is that Camillo was an honest man. And why he left your court, the gods themselves, knowing no more than I, are ignorant.
LEONTES. You knew of his departure, as you know what you undertook to do in his absence.
HERMIONE. Sir, you speak a language I don't understand. My life stands in the line of fire of your dreams, and I'll lay it down.

LEONTES. Your actions are my dreams. You had a bastard by Polixenes, and I only dreamed it. As you were past all shame (those who commit your offense are so), so you are past all truth. Denying it matters more than it helps. For as your brat has been cast out, like itself, with no father owning it (which is, in fact, more criminal in you than in it), so you shall feel our justice, in whose gentlest course you should look for nothing less than death.

HERMIONE. Sir, spare your threats. The bogey you would frighten me with, I seek. To me life can be no benefit. The crown and comfort of my life, your favor, I give up as lost, for I feel it gone, but I don't know how it went. My second joy, the first fruit of my body, I am barred from his presence like someone infectious. My third comfort, born under most unlucky stars, has been dragged from my breast (the innocent milk in its most innocent mouth) to be murdered. I myself am proclaimed a strumpet on every post. With immodest hatred I have been denied the privilege of childbed, which belongs to women of every rank. Lastly, I have been hurried here to this place, into the open air, before I have got strength in my limbs. Now, my liege, tell me what blessings I have here alive, that I should fear to die. Therefore proceed. But hear this first. Don't mistake me. I don't value life a straw, except for my honor, which I would free, if I am to be condemned on guesses, all proofs asleep except what your jealousies awaken. I tell you it is harshness, not law. Your honors all, I refer myself to the oracle. Let Apollo be my judge!
FIRST LORD. This request of yours is altogether just. Therefore bring forth, in Apollo's name, his oracle.
[Exeunt certain Officers.]
HERMIONE. The Emperor of Russia was my father. Oh, if only he were alive, and here to see his daughter's trial! If only he could see the flatness of my misery, but with eyes of pity, not revenge!
[Enter Officers with Cleomenes and Dion.]

OFFICER. You shall swear here upon this sword of justice that you, Cleomenes and Dion, have both been at Delphos, and from there have brought this sealed-up oracle, delivered by the hand of great Apollo's priest. And that since then you have not dared to break the holy seal, nor read the secrets in it.
CLEOMENES, DION. All this we swear.
LEONTES. Break the seals and read.
OFFICER.
[_Reads._] "Hermione is chaste; Polixenes blameless; Camillo a true
subject; Leontes a jealous tyrant; his innocent baby truly begotten; and the king shall live without an heir, if that which is lost is not found."
LORDS. Now blessed be the great Apollo!
HERMIONE. Praised!
LEONTES. Have you read the truth?
OFFICER. Yes, my lord, exactly as it is set down here.
LEONTES. There is no truth at all in the oracle. The session shall proceed. This is pure falsehood.
[Enter a Servant hastily.]
SERVANT. My lord the king, the king!
LEONTES. What is the matter?
SERVANT. Oh sir, I shall be hated for reporting it. The prince your son, from pure imagination and fear for the queen's fate, is gone.
LEONTES. What! Gone?
SERVANT. Is dead.
LEONTES. Apollo is angry, and the heavens themselves strike at my injustice.
[Hermione faints.]
What is it there?
PAULINA. This news is deadly to the queen. Look down and see what death is doing.
LEONTES. Take her away. Her heart is only overcharged. She will recover. I have believed my own suspicion too much. I beg you, tenderly apply to her some remedies for life.
[Exeunt Paulina and Ladies with Hermione.]

Apollo, pardon my great profaneness against your oracle! I'll reconcile myself to Polixenes, woo my queen anew, and recall the good Camillo, whom I proclaim a man of truth and mercy. For, being carried away by my jealousies to bloody thoughts and revenge, I chose Camillo as the agent to poison my friend Polixenes. That would have been done, except that the good mind of Camillo delayed my swift command, though I threatened him with death if he did not do it and encouraged him with reward if it was done. He, most humane and full of honor, unfolded my plot to my kingly guest, gave up his fortunes here, which you knew were great, and committed himself to the certain hazard of all uncertainties, no richer than his honor. How he glitters through my rust! And how his piety makes my deeds the blacker!
[Enter Paulina.]
PAULINA. Woe the while! Oh, cut my lace, lest my heart, cracking it, break too!
FIRST LORD. What fit is this, good lady?

PAULINA. What studied torments, tyrant, do you have for me? What wheels? Racks? Fires? What flaying? Boiling in lead or oils? What old or newer torture must I receive, I whose every word deserves to taste your very worst? Your tyranny, working together with your jealousies, has produced fancies too weak for boys, too green and idle for girls of nine. Oh, think what they have done, and then run mad indeed, stark mad! For all your past foolishness was only spice to it. That you betrayed Polixenes was nothing. That only showed you to be, of a fool, inconstant and damnably ungrateful. Nor was it much that you would have poisoned good Camillo's honor, by having him kill a king. These are poor trespasses, when a more monstrous one stands beside them. Of those I reckon the casting out of your baby daughter to the crows to be little or nothing, though a devil would have shed water out of fire before doing it. Nor is it directly laid to you that the young prince is dead. His honorable thoughts, thoughts too high for one so tender, split the heart that could conceive that a gross and foolish father had blemished his gracious mother. This is not, no, laid to your account. But the last, oh lords, when I have said it, cry Woe! The queen, the queen, the sweetest, dearest creature, is dead, and vengeance for it has not dropped down yet.
FIRST LORD. The higher powers forbid!

PAULINA. I say she's dead. I'll swear it. If neither word nor oath prevails, go and see. If you can bring color or luster to her lip or her eye, warmth outwardly or breath within, I'll serve you as I would serve the gods. But, oh you tyrant! Do not repent these things, for they are heavier than all your woes can stir. Therefore give yourself to nothing but despair. A thousand knees, ten thousand years together, naked, fasting, upon a barren mountain, in constant winter and perpetual storm, could not move the gods to look your way.
LEONTES. Go on, go on. You can't speak too much. I have deserved that all tongues talk their bitterest.
FIRST LORD. Say no more. However the business goes, you have done wrong in the boldness of your speech.

PAULINA. I am sorry for it. All faults I make, when I come to know them, I repent. Alas, I have shown too much of the rashness of a woman. He is touched to the noble heart. What's gone and past help should be past grief. Do not take punishment because of my petition. I beg you, rather let me be punished, who have reminded you of what you should forget. Now, good my liege, sir, royal sir, forgive a foolish woman. The love I bore your queen (look, a fool again!) I'll speak of her no more, nor of your children. I'll not remind you of my own lord, who is lost too. Take your patience to you, and I'll say nothing.

LEONTES. You spoke well when you spoke most truly, and I receive that much better than being pitied by you. Please, take me to the dead bodies of my queen and son. One grave shall be for both. Upon it the causes of their death shall appear, to our perpetual shame. Once a day I'll visit the chapel where they lie, and tears shed there shall be my recreation. As long as nature will bear up under this exercise, so long I vow to practice it daily. Come, and lead me to these sorrows.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 3 — Bohemia. A desert Country near the Sea
paragraphs: [Enter Antigonus with the Child and a Mariner.]
ANTIGONUS. You're sure, then, that our ship has touched the deserts of Bohemia?
MARINER. Yes, my lord, and I fear we've landed at a bad time. The skies look grim and threaten a storm at any moment. I truly believe the heavens are angry at what we have in hand, and frown on us.
ANTIGONUS. Their sacred wills be done! Go, get aboard. Look after your ship. I won't be long before I call for you.
MARINER. Make your best speed, and don't go too far inland. It's likely to be loud weather, and besides, this place is famous for the beasts of prey that live on it.
ANTIGONUS. Go on, away. I'll follow right now.
MARINER. I'm glad at heart to be rid of this business.
[Exit.]

ANTIGONUS. Come, poor baby. I have heard, but never believed, that the spirits of the dead can walk again. If such a thing is possible, your mother appeared to me last night, because there was never a dream so like waking. A figure came to me, her head sometimes on one side, sometimes on the other. I never saw a vessel so full of sorrow, so filled and so becoming. In pure white robes, like holiness itself, she came up to the cabin where I lay. She bowed three times before me, and, gasping to begin some speech, her eyes became two spouts. When the storm of weeping was spent, this broke from her soon after: "Good Antigonus, since fate, against your better nature, has made you the one to throw out my poor baby, according to your oath, there are places remote enough in Bohemia. Weep there, and leave her crying. And because the baby is counted lost forever, I beg you, call her Perdita. For this ungentle business, laid on you by my lord, you will never see your wife Paulina again." And so, with shrieks, she melted into air. I was badly frightened. In time I collected myself and thought this was real, not a dream. Dreams are toys, yet for this once, yes, even superstitiously, I will be guided by this. I do believe Hermione has suffered death, and that Apollo wants this child, being truly the offspring of King Polixenes, to be laid, for life or death, on the soil of her rightful father. Blossom, good luck to you! Lie there, and there is your identifying paper, and there are these things;
[Laying down the child and a bundle.]

which may, if fortune is willing, bring you up, pretty one, and always remain yours. The storm begins. Poor wretch, who for your mother's supposed fault are exposed like this to loss and whatever may follow! I can't weep, but my heart bleeds, and I am most cursed to be bound by oath to this. Farewell! The day frowns more and more. You're likely to have too rough a lullaby. I never saw the heavens so dim by day. A savage clamor! I'd be lucky to get aboard! This is the hunt. I am gone forever.
[Exit, pursued by a bear.]
[Enter an old Shepherd.]

SHEPHERD. I wish there were no age between ten and twenty-three, or that youth would sleep through the rest of it. There's nothing in between but getting girls pregnant, wronging the elders, stealing and fighting. Listen to that now! Would anyone but these boiled brains of nineteen and twenty-two hunt in this weather? They have scared away two of my best sheep, which I fear the wolf will find sooner than their master. If I find them anywhere, it'll be by the seaside, browsing on ivy. Good luck, if it be your will, what have we here?
[Taking up the child.]

Mercy on us, a baby! A very pretty baby! A boy or a girl, I wonder? A pretty one, a very pretty one. Surely some secret escape. Though I'm not bookish, I can read a waiting-gentlewoman in this escape. This was some stair-work, some trunk-work, some behind-the-door work. Whoever made this was warmer than the poor thing is here. I'll pick it up out of pity, but I'll wait till my son comes. He hollered just now. Whoa-ho-hoa!
[Enter Clown.]
CLOWN. Hilloa, loa!
SHEPHERD. What, are you so near? If you want to see something to talk about when you're dead and rotten, come here. What ails you, man?
CLOWN. I have seen two such sights, by sea and by land! But I can't say it's a sea, because now it's the sky. Between the heavens and it, you can't thrust a needle's point.
SHEPHERD. Why, boy, what is it?

CLOWN. I wish you could just see how it chafes, how it rages, how it takes up the shore! But that's beside the point. Oh, the most pitiful cry of the poor souls! Sometimes you see them, and sometimes you don't. Now the ship is boring the moon with her mainmast, and soon she's swallowed up in foam and froth, like pushing a cork into a barrel. And then for the land action, to see how the bear tore out his shoulder-bone, how he cried to me for help, and said his name was Antigonus, a nobleman. But to finish with the ship, to see how the sea swallowed it down like a flap-dragon, a burning raisin gulped from a drink. But first, how the poor souls roared, and the sea mocked them, and how the poor gentleman roared, and the bear mocked him, both roaring louder than the sea or the weather.
SHEPHERD. In the name of mercy, when was this, boy?
CLOWN. Now, now. I haven't blinked since I saw these sights. The men aren't even cold yet under the water, and the bear hasn't half finished dining on the gentleman. He's at it now.
SHEPHERD. I wish I'd been there to help the old man!
CLOWN. I wish you'd been by the ship's side, to help her. Your charity would have had no footing there.

SHEPHERD. Heavy matters, heavy matters! But look here, boy. Now bless yourself. You met things dying, and I met things newborn. Here's a sight for you. Look, a christening cloth for a squire's child! Look here. Pick it up, pick it up, boy. Open it. So, let's see. I was told by the fairies that I'd be rich. This is some changeling. Open it. What's inside, boy?
CLOWN. You're a made old man. If the sins of your youth are forgiven you, you're set for life. Gold! All gold!

SHEPHERD. This is fairy gold, boy, and it will prove to be. Up with it, keep it close. Home, home, the quickest way. We're lucky, boy, and to stay so requires nothing but secrecy. Let my sheep go. Come, good boy, the quickest way home.

CLOWN. You take the quickest way with your findings. I'll go and see if the bear has left the gentleman, and how much he has eaten. Bears are never cruel except when they're hungry. If there's any of him left, I'll bury it.
SHEPHERD. That's a good deed. If you can tell by what's left of him who he is, bring me to see him.
CLOWN. Why, I will, and you shall help me put him in the ground.
SHEPHERD. It's a lucky day, boy, and we'll do good deeds on it.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1
paragraphs: [Enter Time, the Chorus.]

TIME. I who please some and test everyone, who bring both joy and terror to good and bad, who make errors and unfold them, now take it on myself, in the name of Time, to use my wings. Don't count it a crime in me or in my swift passage that I slide over sixteen years and leave unexamined the growth in that wide gap. It is in my power to overthrow law, and in a single self-born hour to plant new custom and overwhelm the old. Let me pass the same as I am, as I was before the most ancient order existed, and before what is accepted now. I witnessed the times that brought those things in, and I shall do the same to the freshest things now reigning. I will make the glitter of this present age grow stale, just as my tale now seems stale to it. If you allow me your patience, I turn my hourglass, and give my scene such growth as if you had slept through the gap between. Leontes has been left with the effects of his foolish jealousies, and grieves so much that he shuts himself away. Imagine me, gentle spectators, now to be in fair Bohemia, and remember well that I mentioned a son of the king's, whom I now name to you as Florizel. I move on quickly to speak of Perdita, now grown in grace to equal the wonder she causes. What follows for her I don't care to prophesy, but let Time's news be known when it is brought forth. A shepherd's daughter, and whatever attaches to her, and whatever follows after, is the subject of Time's tale. Accept this, if you have ever spent time worse before now. If never, still Time himself says he earnestly hopes you never will.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Bohemia. A Room in the palace of Polixenes
paragraphs: [Enter Polixenes and Camillo.]
POLIXENES. Please, good Camillo, stop pressing me. It hurts me to refuse you anything, and it would be death to grant this.

CAMILLO. It's fifteen years since I saw my country. I've spent most of that time abroad, and I want to lay my bones at home. Besides, the repentant king, my master, has sent for me. I might ease his sorrows, or I flatter myself to think so, and that is another reason for me to leave.

POLIXENES. As you love me, Camillo, don't wipe out all your past service by leaving me now. My need of you is the work of your own goodness. It would have been better never to have had you than to lack you like this. You've taken on tasks for me that no one without you can handle properly. So you must either stay and carry them out yourself, or take away with you the very services you've already done. If I haven't thanked you enough for those (and I never could thank you too much), I'll make it my effort to be more grateful, and my gain from it will be the piling up of friendships. Of that fatal country Sicilia, please speak no more. Even naming it punishes me with the memory of that repentant king, as you call him, and reconciled, my brother. The loss of his most precious queen and his children is something he must even now mourn afresh. Tell me, when did you last see Prince Florizel, my son? Kings are no less unhappy when their children turn out badly than when they lose them after those children have proved their virtue.

CAMILLO. Sir, it's three days since I saw the prince. I don't know what his happier business may be. But I have noticed, and missed him, that lately he keeps much away from court and takes part less often in the princely sports than he used to.

POLIXENES. I've noticed that too, Camillo, and with some care. I have eyes in my service watching his withdrawal. They tell me he is seldom away from the house of a very humble shepherd, a man who, they say, has risen from nothing, beyond what his neighbors could imagine, to an extraordinary fortune.
CAMILLO. I've heard of such a man, sir. He has a daughter of very rare reputation. The talk about her goes further than anyone would expect to begin from such a cottage.

POLIXENES. That's also part of my information. But I fear she is the bait that draws our son there. You'll go with us to the place. We'll hide who we are and question the shepherd. From his simplicity I think it won't be hard to learn why my son goes there. Please, be my partner in this business now, and put aside your thoughts of Sicilia.
CAMILLO. I gladly obey your command.
POLIXENES. My best Camillo! We must disguise ourselves.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — The same. A Road near the Shepherd’s cottage
paragraphs: [Enter Autolycus, singing.]
AUTOLYCUS. _When daffodils begin to peek out, With, hey! the girl over the dale, Why, then comes the sweet time of year, For red blood rules over winter's paleness._
_The white sheet bleaching on the hedge, With, hey! the sweet birds, oh, how they sing! Sets my thieving tooth on edge; For a quart of ale is a dish for a king._
_The lark, that sings tirra-lirra, With, hey! with, hey! the thrush and the jay, Are summer songs for me and my aunts, While we lie tumbling in the hay._
I once served Prince Florizel, and in my day I wore three-pile velvet, but now I'm out of work.
_But should I go mourn for that, my dear? The pale moon shines by night: And when I wander here and there, That's when I go most right._
_If tinkers are allowed to live, And carry the sow-skin bag, Then I can well give my account, And swear to it in the stocks._

My trade is sheets. When the kite builds its nest, watch the smaller linen. My father named me Autolycus. He was born under Mercury, as I was, and was likewise a snapper-up of unconsidered trifles. With dice and whores I bought this outfit, and my income is the simple cheat. On the highway, the gallows and the clubbing are too strong for me. Beating and hanging are terrors to me. As for the life to come, I sleep through the thought of it. A prize! A prize!
[Enter Clown.]
CLOWN. Let me see. Every eleven wethers make a tod of wool, and every tod brings in a pound and a few shillings. Fifteen hundred shorn, what does the wool come to?
AUTOLYCUS.
[_Aside._] If the snare holds, the woodcock is mine.

CLOWN. I can't work it out without counters. Let me see, what am I to buy for our sheep-shearing feast? "Three pounds of sugar, five pounds of currants, rice." What will this sister of mine do with rice? But my father has made her mistress of the feast, and she's piling it on. She's had twenty-four nosegays made for the shearers, all singers of three-part songs, and very good ones. But most of them are middle voices and basses, with one puritan among them, and he sings psalms to hornpipes. I must have saffron to color the warden pies. "Mace; dates," none, that's not on my list. "Nutmegs, seven; a race or two of ginger," but I can beg that. "Four pounds of prunes, and as many raisins of the sun."
AUTOLYCUS.
[_Grovelling on the ground._] Oh, that I was ever born!
CLOWN. Bless my soul!
AUTOLYCUS. Oh, help me, help me! Just pull off these rags, and then, death, death!
CLOWN. Alas, poor soul! You need more rags to put on you, not to have these taken off.
AUTOLYCUS. Oh sir, how foul they are offends me more than the blows I've received, which are mighty ones, millions of them.
CLOWN. Alas, poor man! A million blows can add up to a great deal.
AUTOLYCUS. I've been robbed, sir, and beaten. My money and clothes were taken from me, and these detestable things put on me.
CLOWN. What, by a horseman or a footman?
AUTOLYCUS. A footman, sweet sir, a footman.
CLOWN. Indeed, he must have been a footman, judging by the clothes he's left you. If this is a horseman's coat, it's seen very hot service. Give me your hand, I'll help you. Come, give me your hand.
[Helping him up.]
AUTOLYCUS. Oh, good sir, gently, oh!
CLOWN. Alas, poor soul!
AUTOLYCUS. Oh, good sir, softly, good sir. I fear, sir, my shoulder blade is out of joint.
CLOWN. Well now! Can you stand?
AUTOLYCUS. Softly, dear sir! [_Picks his pocket._] Good sir, softly. You've done me a charitable service.
CLOWN. Do you need any money? I have a little money for you.

AUTOLYCUS. No, good sweet sir, no, I beg you, sir. I have a kinsman not more than three-quarters of a mile from here, and I was going to him. I'll have money there, or anything I need. Don't offer me money, please. That kills my heart.
CLOWN. What kind of fellow was he who robbed you?

AUTOLYCUS. A fellow, sir, who I've known to go around with a troll-my-dames game. I knew him once as a servant of the prince. I can't tell, good sir, for which of his virtues it was, but he was certainly whipped out of the court.
CLOWN. His vices, you mean. There's no virtue whipped out of the court. They cherish virtue to make it stay there, and yet it does no more than hang about.

AUTOLYCUS. Vices, I should say, sir. I know this man well. Since then he's been an ape-keeper, then a process-server, a bailiff. Then he put together a puppet show of the Prodigal Son, and married a tinker's wife within a mile of where my land and living lie. And having flown over many knavish trades, he settled on plain rogue. Some call him Autolycus.
CLOWN. Curse him! A thief, I'd stake my life, a thief. He haunts wakes, fairs, and bear-baitings.
AUTOLYCUS. Very true, sir, that's him. That's the rogue who put me into these clothes.
CLOWN. There's not a more cowardly rogue in all Bohemia. If you'd only looked big and spat at him, he'd have run.
AUTOLYCUS. I must confess, sir, I'm no fighter. I'm faint-hearted that way, and he knew it, I'll bet.
CLOWN. How are you now?
AUTOLYCUS. Sweet sir, much better than I was. I can stand and walk. I'll take my leave of you and walk softly toward my kinsman's.
CLOWN. Shall I take you part of the way?
AUTOLYCUS. No, good-faced sir, no, sweet sir.
CLOWN. Then farewell. I must go buy spices for our sheep-shearing.
AUTOLYCUS. Good luck to you, sweet sir!
[Exit Clown.]

Your purse isn't hot enough to pay for your spice. I'll be with you at your sheep-shearing too. If I don't make this cheat hatch another, and the shearers don't prove to be sheep, let me be struck off the roll and my name put in the book of virtue!
[Sings.]
_Jog on, jog on, the footpath way, And merrily step over the stile-a: A merry heart goes all day, A sad one tires in a mile-a._
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — The same. A Shepherd’s Cottage
paragraphs: [Enter Florizel and Perdita.]

FLORIZEL. These unusual clothes of yours give life to every part of you. You're no shepherdess, but Flora peeking out in the first days of April. This sheep-shearing of yours is like a meeting of the minor gods, and you are the queen of it.

PERDITA. Sir, my gracious lord, it isn't right for me to scold your extravagance. Oh, forgive me for naming it! You, the noble mark of the whole land, have hidden yourself in a swain's clothes, and me, a poor lowly girl, you've dressed up like a goddess. But at our feasts every dish has some foolishness in it, and the guests swallow it as a custom. Otherwise I would blush to see you dressed like this. I think I'd faint if I looked at myself in a mirror.
FLORIZEL. I bless the time when my good falcon flew across your father's ground.

PERDITA. Now may Jove give you a reason for that! To me the difference between us brings dread. Your greatness isn't used to fear. Even now I tremble to think your father might by some chance pass this way, as you did. Oh, the Fates! How would he look to see his work, his noble son, so vilely wrapped up? What would he say? Or how could I, in this borrowed finery, face the sternness of his presence?

FLORIZEL. Think of nothing but fun. The gods themselves, lowering their divinity for love, have taken the shapes of beasts. Jupiter became a bull and bellowed. Green Neptune became a ram and bleated. And the fire-robed god, golden Apollo, became a poor humble swain, as I seem now. Their transformations were never for a piece of beauty rarer, nor in a way so chaste, since my desires don't run ahead of my honor, nor do my lusts burn hotter than my faith.

PERDITA. Oh, but sir, your resolution can't hold when it's opposed, as it must be, by the power of the king. One of two things must be necessary, and they will say so: either you must change this purpose, or I must change my life.

FLORIZEL. My dearest Perdita, please don't darken the mirth of the feast with these forced thoughts. Either I'll be yours, my fair one, or I won't be my father's. For I can't be my own, nor anything to anyone, if I'm not yours. I am most constant in this, though destiny says no. Be merry, gentle one. Strangle such thoughts with anything you see around you. Your guests are coming. Lift up your face, as if it were the day of celebration of that wedding we two have sworn will come.
PERDITA. Oh lady Fortune, be on our side!
FLORIZEL. See, your guests are coming. Get ready to welcome them cheerfully, and let's be red with mirth.
[Enter Shepherd with Polixenes and Camillo, disguised; Clown, Mopsa, Dorcas with others.]

SHEPHERD. For shame, daughter! When my old wife was alive, on this day she was pantler, butler and cook, both lady and servant. She welcomed everyone, served everyone, sang her song and danced her turn.
