Now she was at the top of the table, now in the middle, now at one man's shoulder and now another's, her face on fire with work. What she took to cool it, she would sip with each person. You hold back as if you were a guest being feasted, not the hostess of the gathering. Please, bid these unknown friends welcome, for that is a way to make us better friends, better known. Come, quench your blushes and show yourself as what you are, mistress of the feast. Come on, and bid us welcome to your sheep-shearing, so that your good flock will prosper.
PERDITA.
[To Polixenes.] Sir, welcome.
It is my father's will that I take on the hostess's role of the day.
[_To Camillo._] You're welcome, sir.

Give me those flowers there, Dorcas. Reverend sirs, for you there's rosemary and rue. These keep their look and their scent all winter long. Grace and remembrance be with you both! And welcome to our shearing!
POLIXENES. Shepherdess, and a fair one you are, you suit our ages well with flowers of winter.

PERDITA. Sir, the year is growing old, not yet at summer's death nor at the birth of trembling winter. The fairest flowers of the season are our carnations and streaked gillyvors, which some call nature's bastards. Our rustic garden has none of that kind, and I don't care to get cuttings of them.
POLIXENES. Why, gentle maiden, do you neglect them?
PERDITA. Because I've heard it said there is an art which, in their streaked coloring, shares in the work of great creating nature.

POLIXENES. Say there is. Yet nature is made better by no means except what nature itself makes. So that art, which you say adds to nature, is an art that nature makes. You see, sweet maid, we marry a gentler shoot to the wildest stock, and make a bark of baser kind conceive through a bud of nobler race. This is an art that mends nature, or rather changes it. But the art itself is nature.
PERDITA. So it is.
POLIXENES. Then make your garden rich in gillyvors, and don't call them bastards.

PERDITA. I won't put the dibble, the planting stick, into the earth to set one cutting of them. No more than, if I were painted, I would want this young man to say I looked well, and only for that reason desire to have children by me. Here are flowers for you: hot lavender, mints, savory, marjoram, and the marigold, that goes to bed with the sun and rises weeping with him. These are flowers of midsummer, and I think they're given to men of middle age. You're very welcome.
CAMILLO. If I were one of your flock, I would stop grazing and live only by gazing.

PERDITA. Oh, alas! You'd get so lean that the blasts of January would blow right through you. [_To Florizel_] Now, my fairest friend, I wish I had some spring flowers that would suit your time of life, and yours, and yours, who still wear your maidenheads growing on your virgin branches. Oh Proserpina, the flowers you dropped in fright from the wagon of Dis! Daffodils, that come before the swallow dares, and take the winds of March with beauty. Violets, dim, but sweeter than the eyelids of Juno or the breath of Cytherea, which is Venus. Pale primroses, that die unmarried before they can see bright Phoebus in his strength (a sickness most common to maids). Bold oxlips and the crown imperial. Lilies of all kinds, the fleur-de-luce being one. Oh, these I lack, to make you garlands of. And, my sweet friend, to strew over him again and again!
FLORIZEL. What, like a corpse?

PERDITA. No, like a bank for love to lie and play on. Not like a corpse, or if so, not to be buried, but alive, in my arms. Come, take your flowers. I feel I'm playing a part, as I've seen people do in Whitsun pastorals. Surely this robe of mine changes my disposition.

FLORIZEL. Whatever you do always improves on what has been done. When you speak, sweet, I'd want you to do it forever. When you sing, I'd want you to buy and sell like that, so give alms, and pray so, and to manage your affairs by singing them too. When you dance, I wish you were a wave of the sea, so that you could do nothing but that, move on and on like that, and have no other function. Each thing you do, so singular in every detail, crowns what you are doing in the present deed, so that all your acts are queens.

PERDITA. Oh Doricles, your praises are too generous. But if your youth, and the true blood that shows fairly through it, did not plainly declare you an unstained shepherd, I might wisely fear, my Doricles, that you were wooing me the false way.
FLORIZEL. I think you have as little skill in fearing as I have purpose to give you cause. But come, our dance, please. Your hand, my Perdita. So turtledoves pair that never mean to part.
PERDITA. I'll swear for them.
POLIXENES. This is the prettiest low-born girl that ever ran on the green grass. Nothing she does or seems to do but smacks of something greater than herself, too noble for this place.
CAMILLO. He's telling her something that makes her blood show in her cheeks. In truth, she is the queen of curds and cream.
CLOWN. Come on, strike up.
DORCAS. Mopsa must be your partner. Why, garlic, to improve her kissing!
MOPSA. Well, really!
CLOWN. Not a word, not a word. We stand on our manners. Come, strike up.
[Music. Here a dance of Shepherds and Shepherdesses.]
POLIXENES. Please, good shepherd, what fair swain is this who dances with your daughter?

SHEPHERD. They call him Doricles, and he boasts of having good pasture. But I have that only from his own report, and I believe it. He looks honest. He says he loves my daughter. I think so too, for the moon never gazed on the water as he will stand and read my daughter's eyes. And to be plain, there's not half a kiss to choose between them as to which loves the other best.
POLIXENES. She dances neatly.
SHEPHERD. So she does anything, though I who should be silent say so. If young Doricles wins her, she'll bring him what he doesn't dream of.
[Enter a Servant.]

SERVANT. Oh master, if you could only hear the pedlar at the door, you would never dance again to a tabor and pipe. No, even the bagpipe couldn't move you. He sings several tunes faster than you can count money. He pours them out as if he had eaten ballads, and all men's ears had grown to his tunes.
CLOWN. He couldn't come at a better time. Let him come in. I love a ballad all too well, if it's sad matter set down merrily, or a very pleasant thing sung mournfully.

SERVANT. He has songs for men or women of all sizes. No milliner can fit his customers so well with gloves. He has the prettiest love-songs for maids, so free of bawdry, which is strange. They have such delicate refrains of "dildos" and "fadings," and "jump her and thump her." And where some wide-mouthed rascal would mean mischief and break a foul gap into the matter, he makes the maid answer "Whoop, do me no harm, good man," and puts him off, slights him, with "Whoop, do me no harm, good man."
POLIXENES. This is a fine fellow.
CLOWN. Believe me, you're talking of a wonderfully clever fellow. Does he have any good, unfaded wares?

SERVANT. He has ribbons in all the colors of the rainbow. He has points, the laces, more than all the lawyers in Bohemia could learnedly handle, though they come to him by the gross. He has linen tapes, worsted braids, cambrics, lawns. Why, he sings them over as if they were gods or goddesses. You would think a smock was a she-angel, the way he chants about the sleeve-band and the embroidery around its square panel.
CLOWN. Please bring him in, and let him come singing.
PERDITA. Warn him not to use any scurrilous words in his tunes.
[Exit Servant.]
CLOWN. You get some of these pedlars who have more in them than you'd think, sister.
PERDITA. Yes, good brother, or even try to think.
[Enter Autolycus, singing.]

AUTOLYCUS. _Lawn as white as driven snow, Cypress black as ever was crow, Gloves as sweet as damask roses, Masks for faces and for noses, Bugle-bracelet, necklace amber, Perfume for a lady's chamber, Golden coifs and stomachers For my lads to give their dears, Pins and poking-sticks of steel, What maids lack from head to heel. Come buy of me, come; come buy, come buy; Buy, lads, or else your lasses cry. Come, buy._
CLOWN. If I weren't in love with Mopsa, you would get no money from me. But being as enthralled as I am, it will also be the bondage of certain ribbons and gloves.
MOPSA. I was promised them for the feast, but they don't come too late now.
DORCAS. He has promised you more than that, or there are liars about.
MOPSA. He's paid you everything he promised you. Maybe he's paid you more, which you'd be ashamed to give back to him.

CLOWN. Is there no manners left among maids? Will they wear their petticoat slits where they should wear their faces? Isn't there milking-time, when you're going to bed, or the kiln-hole, to whisper about these secrets, without your tittle-tattling in front of all our guests? It's good they're whispering. Hold your tongues, and not a word more.
MOPSA. I've done. Come, you promised me a tawdry lace and a pair of sweet gloves.
CLOWN. Haven't I told you how I was cheated on the way and lost all my money?
AUTOLYCUS. And indeed, sir, there are cheats about, so men should be wary.
CLOWN. Don't worry, man. You'll lose nothing here.
AUTOLYCUS. I hope so, sir, for I have about me many parcels of value.
CLOWN. What have you here? Ballads?
MOPSA. Please now, buy some. I love a printed ballad dearly, for then we're sure they're true.
AUTOLYCUS. Here's one to a very sad tune. How a moneylender's wife gave birth to twenty money-bags at one go, and how she longed to eat adders' heads and grilled toads.
MOPSA. Is it true, do you think?
AUTOLYCUS. Very true, and only a month old.
DORCAS. Bless me from marrying a usurer!
AUTOLYCUS. Here's the midwife's name on it, one Mistress Taleporter, and five or six honest wives who were present. Why should I carry lies around?
MOPSA. Please now, buy it.
CLOWN. Come on, put it aside, and let's see more ballads first. We'll buy the other things soon.

AUTOLYCUS. Here's another ballad, of a fish that appeared on the coast on Wednesday the eightieth of April, forty thousand fathoms above water, and sang this ballad against the hard hearts of maids. It was thought she was a woman, and was turned into a cold fish because she would not exchange flesh with one who loved her. The ballad is very pitiful, and as true.
DORCAS. Is it true too, do you think?
AUTOLYCUS. Five justices' hands on it, and more witnesses than my pack will hold.
CLOWN. Put it aside too. Another.
AUTOLYCUS. This is a merry ballad, but a very pretty one.
MOPSA. Let's have some merry ones.
AUTOLYCUS. Why, this is an exceedingly merry one, and it goes to the tune of "Two maids wooing a man." Hardly a maid in the west doesn't sing it. It's in demand, I can tell you.
MOPSA. We can both sing it. If you'll take a part, you shall hear it. It's in three parts.
DORCAS. We had the tune of it a month ago.
AUTOLYCUS. I can take my part. You must know it's my trade. Have at it with you.
SONG.
AUTOLYCUS. _Get away from here, for I must go where it's not fit for you to know._
DORCAS. _Where?_
MOPSA. _Oh, where?_
DORCAS. _Where?_
MOPSA. _It suits your oath well that you tell me your secrets._
DORCAS. _Me too! Let me go there._
MOPSA. Or you're going to the farm or the mill.
DORCAS. _If to either, you do wrong._
AUTOLYCUS. _Neither._
DORCAS. _What, neither?_
AUTOLYCUS. _Neither._
DORCAS. _You swore to be my love._
MOPSA. _You swore it even more to me. So where are you going? Say, where?_

CLOWN. We'll have this song out later by ourselves. My father and the gentlemen are in serious talk, and we won't disturb them. Come, bring your pack along after me. Girls, I'll buy for you both. Pedlar, let us have first choice. Follow me, girls.
[Exit with Dorcas and Mopsa.]
AUTOLYCUS.
[_Aside._] And you shall pay well for them.
SONG.

_Will you buy any tape, Or lace for your cape, My dainty duck, my dear-a? Any silk, any thread, Any toys for your head, Of the newest and finest, finest wear-a? Come to the pedlar; Money's a meddler That sells off all men's ware-a._
[Exit.]
[Enter Servant.]

SERVANT. Master, there are three carters, three shepherds, three cowherds, three swineherds, who have made themselves all hairy men. They call themselves saltiers, and they have a dance which the girls say is a gallimaufry of gambols, because they aren't in it. But the men themselves think (if it's not too rough for some who know little but bowling) that it will please plentifully.
SHEPHERD. Away! We'll have none of it. There's been too much homely foolery already. I know, sir, we weary you.
POLIXENES. You weary those who refresh us. Please, let's see these four threes of herdsmen.
SERVANT. One three of them, by their own report, sir, has danced before the king, and the least of the three jumps twelve and a half feet by the measure.
SHEPHERD. Stop your prattling. Since these good men are pleased, let them come in, but quickly now.
SERVANT. Why, they're waiting at the door, sir.
[Exit.]
[Enter Twelve Rustics, dressed like Satyrs. They dance, and then exeunt.]
POLIXENES. Oh, father, you'll hear more of that later.
[_To Camillo._] Isn't it gone too far? It's time to part them.

He's simple and tells a lot. [_To Florizel._] How now, fair shepherd! Your heart is full of something that takes your mind from feasting. Truly, when I was young and held hands in love as you do, I used to load my sweetheart with trinkets. I would have ransacked the pedlar's silken treasury and poured it out for her to accept. You've let him go and bought nothing from him. If your girl should misinterpret this and call it your lack of love or generosity, you'd be hard pressed for a reply, at least if you care about holding her happily.

FLORIZEL. Old sir, I know she doesn't prize trifles like these. The gifts she looks for from me are packed and locked up in my heart, which I have given already, but not delivered. Oh, hear me breathe out my life before this old gentleman, who, it seems, has loved at some time. I take your hand! This hand, as soft as dove's down and as white as it, or as an Ethiopian's tooth, or the winnowed snow that's been sifted twice over by the northern blasts.
POLIXENES. What follows this? How prettily the young swain seems to wash the hand that was fair before! I've put you off. But go on with your protestation. Let me hear what you profess.
FLORIZEL. Do, and be witness to it.
POLIXENES. And this my neighbor too?

FLORIZEL. And he, and more than he, and men, the earth, the heavens, and all. If I were crowned the most imperial monarch, the most worthy of it, if I were the fairest youth who ever made an eye swerve, had more strength and knowledge than any man ever had, I would not prize them without her love. For her sake I would use them all, commit them and condemn them to her service, or to their own ruin.
POLIXENES. Fairly offered.
CAMILLO. This shows a sound affection.
SHEPHERD. But my daughter, do you say the same to him?
PERDITA. I can't speak so well, nowhere near so well, no, nor mean better. By the pattern of my own thoughts I cut out the purity of his.
SHEPHERD. Take hands, a bargain! And, friends unknown, you shall bear witness to it. I give my daughter to him, and will make her dowry equal to his.

FLORIZEL. Oh, that must come through your daughter's worth. Once one man is dead, I shall have more than you can dream of yet. Enough then for your wonder. But come on, contract us before these witnesses.
SHEPHERD. Come, your hand. And, daughter, yours.
POLIXENES. Wait, swain, a moment, I beg you. Have you a father?
FLORIZEL. I have. But what of him?
POLIXENES. Does he know of this?
FLORIZEL. He doesn't, and he won't.

POLIXENES. I think a father is the guest who best graces the table at his son's wedding. Please, once more, has your father become unfit for ordinary business? Is he not dulled with age and with the changing humors of old men's rheums? Can he speak? Hear? Tell one man from another? Argue about his own estate? Does he lie bedridden? And does he do nothing again but what he did as a child?
FLORIZEL. No, good sir. He has his health, and indeed more strength than most men of his age.

POLIXENES. By my white beard, if that's so, you do him a wrong, somewhat unfilial. It's reasonable that a son should choose his own wife, but just as reasonable that the father, whose only joy is fair descendants, should have some say in such a business.
FLORIZEL. I grant all this. But for some other reasons, my grave sir, which it isn't fit for you to know, I don't tell my father of this business.
POLIXENES. Let him know it.
FLORIZEL. He shall not.
POLIXENES. Please, let him.
FLORIZEL. No, he must not.
SHEPHERD. Let him, my son. He won't need to grieve at knowing your choice.
FLORIZEL. Come, come, he must not. Mark our contract.
POLIXENES.
[Revealing himself.] Mark your divorce, young sir,

whom I dare not call son. You are too base to be acknowledged. You, a sceptre's heir, who go for a sheep-hook like this! You, old traitor, I'm sorry that by hanging you I can only shorten your life by one week. And you, fresh piece of excellent witchcraft, who must surely know the royal fool you're dealing with,
SHEPHERD. Oh, my heart!

POLIXENES. I'll have your beauty scratched with briars and made plainer than your station. As for you, foolish boy, if I ever learn that you so much as sigh because you will no longer see this trinket (as I mean you never shall), we'll bar you from the succession. We won't hold you of our blood, no, not our kin, no, farther off than Deucalion. Mark my words. Follow us to the court. You churl, for this time, though full of our displeasure, we free you from the deadly blow of it. And you, enchantment, good enough for a herdsman; yes, even for him, who makes himself one, and who, apart from our honor in him, is unworthy of you. If ever from now on you open these rural latches to his entrance, or hoop his body with your embraces, I will devise a death as cruel for you as you are tender to it.
[Exit.]

PERDITA. Undone, even here. I wasn't very afraid, for once or twice I was about to speak and tell him plainly that the same sun that shines on his court doesn't hide its face from our cottage, but looks on both alike. [_To Florizel._] Will it please you, sir, to go? I told you what would come of this. I beg you, take care of your own position. This dream of mine, now that I'm awake, I'll play queen no farther, but milk my ewes, and weep.
CAMILLO. Why, how now, father! Speak before you die.

SHEPHERD. I can't speak, nor think, nor dare to know what I know. Oh sir, you have undone a man of eighty-three, who thought to fill his grave in quiet, yes, to die on the bed my father died on, to lie close by his honest bones. But now some hangman must put on my shroud and lay me where no priest shovels in dust. Oh cursed wretch, who knew this was the prince and dared to pledge faith to him! Undone, undone! If I might die within this hour, I have lived to die when I desire.
[Exit.]

FLORIZEL. Why do you look at me so? I'm only sorry, not afraid. Delayed, but nothing altered. What I was, I am. I strain on all the more for being pulled back, and I don't follow my leash unwillingly.

CAMILLO. My gracious lord, you know your father's temper. At this time he will allow no speech (which I guess you don't intend to give him), and he will hardly bear the sight of you yet, I fear. So until the fury of his highness settles, don't come before him.
FLORIZEL. I don't intend it. I think it's Camillo?
CAMILLO. Even he, my lord.
PERDITA. How often have I told you it would be like this! How often I said my rank would last only until it was found out!

FLORIZEL. It can only fail if I break my faith. And if I do, then let nature crush the two sides of the earth together and ruin the seeds inside it! Lift up your face. Wipe me out of the line of succession, father. I am heir to my own love.
CAMILLO. Think carefully.
FLORIZEL. I am, and by my own heart's choice. If my reason will obey that, then I have reason on my side. If not, my senses, happier with madness, welcome it.
CAMILLO. This is desperate, sir.

FLORIZEL. Call it that. But it fulfills my vow, and I have to think it honorable. Camillo, not for Bohemia, nor for all the glory that could be gathered from it, nor for everything the sun sees, the solid earth holds in its womb, or the deep seas hide in unknown depths, will I break my oath to my beautiful beloved. So I ask you, as you have always been my father's honored friend: when he misses me (and I truly mean never to see him again), turn your good advice on his anger. Let me and my fortune struggle over what comes next. You may tell him this: I am putting out to sea with her, whom I cannot keep here on shore. And, just when she needs it, I have a ship riding close by, though it is not fitted out for this plan. The course I mean to take will do you no good to know, and it does not concern me to report it.
CAMILLO. Oh my lord, I wish your spirit were more open to advice, or stronger for your need.
FLORIZEL. Listen, Perdita. [_Takes her aside._]
[_To Camillo._] I'll hear you in a moment.

CAMILLO. He can't be moved. He's determined to flee. Now I would be happy if I could arrange his going to serve my own purpose: save him from danger, show him love and honor, and win back the sight of dear Sicilia and that unhappy king, my master, whom I long so much to see.
FLORIZEL. Now, good Camillo, I am so loaded with pressing business that I leave out ceremony.
CAMILLO. Sir, I think you have heard of my humble services, in the love I have borne your father?
FLORIZEL. Very nobly have you earned his thanks. It is music to my father to speak of your deeds, and he takes no small care to repay them as he thinks of them.

CAMILLO. Well, my lord, if you will believe that I love the king, and, through him, what is nearest to him, which is your gracious self, then take my direction, if your weighty and settled plan can bear any change. On my honor, I'll point you to a place where you will be received as befits your highness, and where you can enjoy your mistress. I see there is no separating you from her, except by, which heaven forbid, your ruin. Marry her. And while you are away, I'll do my best to soften your displeased father and bring him around to approval.
FLORIZEL. How, Camillo, can this be done? It is almost a miracle. Tell me, so I can call you something more than a man, and after that trust you.
CAMILLO. Have you thought of a place where you'll go?
FLORIZEL. Not any yet. But just as some unforeseen accident is to blame for what we do so wildly, so we declare ourselves slaves of chance, and flies of every wind that blows.

CAMILLO. Then listen to me. This follows, if you will not change your purpose and will go through with this flight: make for Sicilia, and present yourself and your fair princess to Leontes. For I see she must be a princess. She shall be dressed as suits the partner of your bed. I think I see Leontes opening his generous arms and weeping out his welcomes. He asks you, the son, for forgiveness, as if you were your father in person. He kisses the hands of your young princess. Over and over he divides himself between his unkindness and his kindness. The one he scolds to hell, and the other he bids grow faster than thought or time.
FLORIZEL. Worthy Camillo, what excuse for my visit shall I hold up before him?

CAMILLO. That you were sent by the king your father to greet him and to give him comfort. Sir, as for how you behave toward him, and what you (as if from your father) shall say, the things known among us three, I'll write them down for you. They will show you at every sitting what you must say. He won't see anything but that you have your father's confidence there and speak his very heart.
FLORIZEL. I am in your debt. There is some life in this.

CAMILLO. It's a course more promising than a wild dedication of yourselves to uncharted waters and undreamed-of shores. That is certain to bring misery enough, with no hope to help you, except when you shake off one trouble to take on another. Nothing is as certain as your anchors, which do their best work if they can only hold you where you'll be loath to be. Besides, you know prosperity is the very bond of love, and hardship changes both its fresh complexion and its heart together.
PERDITA. One of these is true. I think hardship may wear down the cheek, but not take over the mind.
CAMILLO. Oh, do you say so? There will not be born another like her at your father's house in these seven years.
FLORIZEL. My good Camillo, she is as far ahead in her breeding as she is behind in her birth.
CAMILLO. I can't say it's a pity she lacks teaching, for she seems a mistress to most who teach.
PERDITA. Your pardon, sir. For this I'll blush my thanks.

FLORIZEL. My prettiest Perdita! But oh, the thorns we stand on! Camillo, preserver of my father, and now of me, the medicine of our house, what shall we do? We are not equipped like Bohemia's son, and we won't look like him in Sicilia.

CAMILLO. My lord, fear none of this. I think you know my fortunes all lie there. It will be my care to have you royally outfitted, as if the part you play were mine. For instance, sir, so you know you will not lack anything — one word.
[They talk aside.]
[Enter Autolycus.]

AUTOLYCUS. Ha, ha! What a fool Honesty is! And Trust, his sworn brother, a very simple gentleman! I have sold all my trumpery. Not a fake stone, not a ribbon, mirror, scent-ball, brooch, notebook, ballad, knife, tape, glove, shoe-tie, bracelet, horn-ring is left to keep my pack from going hungry. They crowded to be first to buy, as if my trinkets had been blessed and brought a benediction to the buyer. That's how I saw whose purse was best to look at, and what I saw I remembered to my good use. My Clown (who lacks only a little to be a reasonable man) fell so in love with the girls' song that he wouldn't stir his pig's feet until he had both tune and words. That drew the rest of the herd to me, so that all their other senses stuck in their ears. You could have pinched a petticoat-slit and they wouldn't have felt it. It was nothing to cut a purse off a codpiece. I could have filed keys off their chains. No hearing, no feeling, only my fine fellow's song and admiring the nothing of it. So in this time of stupor I picked and cut most of their festival purses. And if the old man hadn't come in with an uproar against his daughter and the king's son, and scared my crows from the chaff, I wouldn't have left a purse alive in the whole army.
[Camillo, Florizel and Perdita come forward.]
CAMILLO. No, but my letters, being there as soon as you arrive, will clear that doubt.
FLORIZEL. And those that you'll get from King Leontes?
CAMILLO. Will satisfy your father.
PERDITA. Happy be you! All that you say looks good.
CAMILLO.
[Seeing Autolycus.] Who have we here?
We'll make a tool of this one. Let's miss nothing that might help us.
AUTOLYCUS.
[_Aside._] If they have overheard me now — why, hanging.
CAMILLO. How now, good fellow! Why are you shaking so? Don't be afraid, man. No harm is intended to you here.
AUTOLYCUS. I am a poor fellow, sir.

CAMILLO. Why, stay so. Nobody here will steal that from you. But we must make an exchange for the outside of your poverty. So strip yourself at once (you must think there's a need for it) and change clothes with this gentleman. Though he gets the worse of the bargain, still, take this, there's some extra to make up.
[Giving money.]
AUTOLYCUS. I am a poor fellow, sir. [_Aside._] I know you well enough.
CAMILLO. No, please, hurry. The gentleman is half stripped already.
AUTOLYCUS. Are you serious, sir? [_Aside._] I smell the trick in it.
FLORIZEL. Hurry, please.
AUTOLYCUS. Indeed, I have been paid in advance, but I can't with a clear conscience take it.
CAMILLO. Unbuckle, unbuckle.
[Florizel and Autolycus exchange clothes.]

Fortunate mistress (let my prophecy come true for you!), you must hide yourself in some cover. Take your sweetheart's hat and pull it down over your brows, muffle your face, undress yourself, and as best you can, make your true appearance unlike itself. That way, for I fear watching eyes everywhere, you can get to the ship unseen.
PERDITA. I see the play is written so that I must play a part.
CAMILLO. No help for it. Have you finished there?
FLORIZEL. If I met my father now, he wouldn't call me son.
CAMILLO. No, you shall have no hat. [_Giving it to Perdita._] Come, lady, come. Farewell, my friend.
AUTOLYCUS. Goodbye, sir.
FLORIZEL. Oh Perdita, what have we two forgotten? Please, a word.
[They converse apart.]
CAMILLO.
[_Aside._] What I do next will be to tell the king
Of this escape and where they are headed. My hope is to persuade him to follow them. In his company I shall see Sicilia again, and I have a woman's longing for the sight of it.
FLORIZEL. Fortune speed us! So we set out, Camillo, to the seaside.
CAMILLO. The faster the better.
[Exeunt Florizel, Perdita and Camillo.]

AUTOLYCUS. I understand the business. I hear it. To have an open ear, a quick eye and a nimble hand is necessary for a cutpurse. A good nose is also required, to sniff out work for the other senses. I see this is the time when the unjust man thrives. What an exchange this would have been without the extra money! What an extra there is with this exchange! Surely the gods this year are winking at us, and we can do anything on the spur of the moment. The prince himself is up to a piece of wickedness, stealing away from his father with his ball and chain at his heels. If I thought it would be an honest act to tell the king about it, I wouldn't do it. I hold it more knavery to conceal it, and in that I am true to my profession.
[Enter Clown and Shepherd.]
Aside, aside. Here is more matter for a hot brain. Every lane's end, every shop, church, court session and hanging gives a watchful man work.
CLOWN. See, see, what a man you are now! There's no other way but to tell the king she's a changeling, and none of your flesh and blood.
SHEPHERD. No, but hear me.
CLOWN. No, but hear me.
SHEPHERD. Go on, then.

CLOWN. She being none of your flesh and blood, your flesh and blood hasn't offended the king. So your flesh and blood is not to be punished by him. Show him those things you found with her, those secret things, everything but what she has on her. Once that's done, let the law go whistle, I promise you.
SHEPHERD. I will tell the king everything, every word, yes, and his son's pranks too. He is, I may say, no honest man either to his father or to me, going about to make me the king's brother-in-law.
CLOWN. Indeed, brother-in-law was the farthest off you could have been to him, and then your blood would have been dearer by I don't know how much an ounce.
AUTOLYCUS.
[Aside.] Very wisely, puppies!
SHEPHERD. Well, let's go to the king. There is something in this bundle that will make him scratch his beard.
AUTOLYCUS.
[_Aside._] I don't know what obstacle this complaint may be to the
flight of my master.
CLOWN. I sincerely hope he's at the palace.
AUTOLYCUS.
[_Aside._] Though I'm not honest by nature, I am sometimes by
chance. Let me pocket up my pedlar's junk. [_Takes off his false beard._] Well now, country folk! Where are you headed?
SHEPHERD. To the palace, if it please your worship.
AUTOLYCUS. Your business there: what, with whom, what's in that bundle, where you live, your names, your ages, your property, your upbringing, and anything else that's fit to be known. Out with it!
CLOWN. We are only plain fellows, sir.

AUTOLYCUS. A lie. You are rough and hairy. Let me have no lying. Lying suits only tradesmen, and they often give us soldiers the lie. But we pay them for it with stamped coin, not stabbing steel, so they don't give us the lie.
CLOWN. Your worship nearly gave us one, if you hadn't caught yourself in the act.
SHEPHERD. Are you a courtier, if it please you, sir?

AUTOLYCUS. Whether it pleases me or not, I am a courtier. Don't you see the air of the court in these clothes? Doesn't my walk have the measure of the court in it? Doesn't your nose pick up the court's perfume from me? Don't I cast court contempt on your lowness? Do you think that because I worm my way in and wheedle your business out of you, I'm therefore no courtier? I am a courtier _cap-a-pe_, from head to foot, and one who will either push your business forward or hold it back. So I command you to lay open your affair.
SHEPHERD. My business, sir, is with the king.
AUTOLYCUS. What advocate do you have with him?
SHEPHERD. I don't know, if it please you.
CLOWN. "Advocate" is the court word for a pheasant. Say you have none.
SHEPHERD. None, sir. I have no pheasant, cock or hen.
AUTOLYCUS. How blessed we are, who are not simple men! Yet nature might have made me like these, so I will not look down on them.
CLOWN. This can't be anything but a great courtier.
SHEPHERD. His clothes are rich, but he doesn't wear them handsomely.
CLOWN. He seems all the nobler for being so fanciful. A great man, I'll bet. I can tell by how he picks his teeth.
AUTOLYCUS. That bundle there? What's in the bundle? Why that box?
SHEPHERD. Sir, there are such secrets in this bundle and box that none must know them but the king. And he shall know them within this hour, if I can get to speak with him.
AUTOLYCUS. Old man, you've wasted your effort.
SHEPHERD. Why, sir?
AUTOLYCUS. The king is not at the palace. He has gone aboard a new ship to purge his melancholy and take the air. For if you're able to grasp serious things, you must know the king is full of grief.
SHEPHERD. So it's said, sir. About his son, who was to have married a shepherd's daughter.
AUTOLYCUS. If that shepherd isn't already in custody, let him run. The curses he will get, the tortures he will feel, will break the back of a man and the heart of a monster.
CLOWN. Do you think so, sir?

AUTOLYCUS. Not he alone will suffer what wit can make heavy and vengeance bitter. Those who are related to him, though removed fifty times, will all come under the hangman. That is a great pity, but it is necessary. An old sheep-whistling rogue, a ram-tender, to try to bring his daughter into royal favor! Some say he will be stoned, but that death is too soft for him, I say. Drag our throne into a sheepfold! All deaths are too few, the sharpest too easy.
CLOWN. Does the old man have a son, sir, do you know, if it please you, sir?

AUTOLYCUS. He has a son, who will be flayed alive. Then he'll be smeared over with honey and set on top of a wasp's nest. Then he'll stand there until he's three quarters and a dram dead. Then he'll be revived with brandy or some other hot drink. Then, raw as he is, on the hottest day the almanac predicts, he will be set against a brick wall, with the sun looking at him with a southward eye, and there he will watch the flies blow on him until he dies. But why do we talk of these treacherous rascals, whose miseries are to be smiled at, their offenses being so serious? Tell me (for you seem to be honest, plain men) what you have for the king. If I'm rewarded handsomely, I'll bring you to where he is aboard ship, present you to him, whisper a word for you. And if anyone besides the king can get your suits done, here is the man who will do it.

CLOWN. He seems to be a man of great authority. Close with him, give him gold. And though authority is a stubborn bear, it's often led by the nose with gold. Show the inside of your purse to the outside of his hand, and no more fuss. Remember: "stoned" and "flayed alive."
SHEPHERD. If it please you, sir, to undertake the business for us, here is the gold I have. I'll make it as much again, and leave this young man in pawn until I bring it to you.
AUTOLYCUS. After I have done what I promised?
SHEPHERD. Yes, sir.
AUTOLYCUS. Well, give me the half. Are you a party in this business?
CLOWN. In some sort, sir. But though my case is a pitiful one, I hope I won't be flayed out of it.
AUTOLYCUS. Oh, that's the case of the shepherd's son. Hang him, he'll be made an example.

CLOWN. Comfort, good comfort! We must go to the king and show him our strange sights. He must know she's none of your daughter and no sister of mine, or we're done for. Sir, I will give you as much as this old man does when the business is done, and remain, as he says, your pawn until it's brought to you.
AUTOLYCUS. I will trust you. Walk ahead toward the seaside. Go on the right-hand side. I'll just look at the hedge, and follow you.
CLOWN. We are blessed in this man, as I may say, even blessed.
SHEPHERD. Let's go ahead, as he tells us. He was sent to do us good.
[Exeunt Shepherd and Clown.]

AUTOLYCUS. If I had a mind to be honest, I see Fortune wouldn't allow it. She drops loot into my mouth. I am courted now by a double opportunity: gold, and a means of doing the prince my master a good turn, which, who knows, may turn back to my advancement. I will bring these two moles, these blind ones, aboard to him. If he thinks fit to put them ashore again, and the complaint they have for the king doesn't concern him at all, let him call me a rogue for being so far too eager. For I am proof against that title and whatever shame goes with it. I will present them to him. There may be something in it.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Sicilia. A Room in the palace of Leontes
paragraphs: [Enter Leontes, Cleomenes, Dion, Paulina and others.]

CLEOMENES Sir, you have done enough, and have carried out a saintly sorrow. There is no fault you could commit that you haven't made up for. Indeed, you have paid more penance than the wrong you did. At last, do as the heavens have done: forget your sin. With them, forgive yourself.

LEONTES. While I remember her and her virtues, I cannot forget my faults against them. So I keep thinking of the wrong I did myself, which was so great that it has left my kingdom without an heir, and destroyed the sweetest companion a man ever grew his hopes from.

PAULINA. True, too true, my lord. If you married every woman in the world, one by one, or took something good from all of them to make one perfect woman, the one you killed would still be without equal.
LEONTES. I think so. Killed! She I killed! I did so. But you strike me painfully to say I did. It is as bitter on your tongue as in my thought. Now, please, say it only seldom.
CLEOMENES Not at all, good lady. You might have said a thousand things that would have done the times more good and shown your kindness better.
PAULINA. You are one of those who would have him marry again.

DION. If you would not, you have no pity for the state, nor for the memory of his most sovereign name. You give little thought to what dangers, through his highness's failure to have a child, may fall on his kingdom and devour the uncertain onlookers. What could be more holy than to rejoice that the former queen is at peace? What holier than, for the repair of the royal line, for present comfort and for future good, to bless the bed of majesty again with a sweet partner to it?

PAULINA. There is none worthy, compared with her who is gone. Besides, the gods will have fulfilled their secret purposes. For hasn't the divine Apollo said, isn't it the tenor of his oracle, that King Leontes shall not have an heir until his lost child is found? That this should happen is as monstrous to our human reason as my Antigonus breaking out of his grave and coming back to me, who, on my life, died with the infant. It is your advice that would have my lord go against the heavens and oppose their will. [_To Leontes._] Don't worry about an heir. The crown will find one. Great Alexander left his to the worthiest, so his successor was likely to be the best.

LEONTES. Good Paulina, you who keep the memory of Hermione, I know, in honor. Oh, that I had ever shaped myself by your advice! Then, even now, I might have looked into my queen's full eyes, and taken treasure from her lips —
PAULINA. And left them more rich for what they gave.

LEONTES. You speak the truth. No more such wives, and therefore no wife. One worse, and better treated, would make her sainted spirit take over her corpse again and, on this stage where we offenders now appear, soul-tormented, begin with "Why to me?"
PAULINA. Had she such power, she would have just cause.
LEONTES. She would. And she would enrage me into murdering the woman I married.

PAULINA. I would. If I were the ghost that walked, I'd tell you to look at her eye, and tell me for what dull fault in it you chose her. Then I'd shriek so that even your ears would split to hear me, and the words that followed would be "Remember mine."
LEONTES. Stars, stars, and all other eyes dead coals! Don't fear I'll take a wife. I'll have no wife, Paulina.
PAULINA. Will you swear never to marry except with my free leave?
LEONTES. Never, Paulina. So may my spirit be blessed!
PAULINA. Then, my good lords, bear witness to his oath.
CLEOMENES You tempt him too much.
PAULINA. Unless another woman, as like Hermione as her portrait is, comes before his eyes.
CLEOMENES Good madam —

PAULINA. I have done. Yet if my lord will marry (if you will, sir, and there's no help but you will), give me the task of choosing you a queen. She will not be as young as your former one, but she will be such that, if your first queen's ghost walked, it would take joy in seeing her in your arms.
LEONTES. My true Paulina, we shall not marry until you bid us.
PAULINA. That will be when your first queen breathes again. Never until then.
[Enter a Servant.]
SERVANT. One who gives out that he is Prince Florizel, son of Polixenes, with his princess (the fairest I have yet seen), asks to be admitted to your high presence.

LEONTES. What is he doing here? He doesn't come like his father's greatness. His arrival, so out of the ordinary and sudden, tells us this is not a planned visit but one forced by need and accident. What retinue?
SERVANT. Very few, and those poor.
LEONTES. His princess, you say, is with him?
SERVANT. Yes, the most peerless piece of earth, I think, that the sun ever shone brightly on.

PAULINA. Oh Hermione, as every present time boasts itself above a better one gone, so your grave must give way to what is seen now! Sir, you yourself have said and written so, but your writing now is colder than that theme: "She had not been, nor was she ever to be, equaled." So your verse once flowed with her beauty. It has ebbed badly, if you say you have seen a better.

SERVANT. Pardon, madam. The one I have almost forgotten (your pardon). The other, when she has caught your eye, will have your tongue too. This is a creature who, if she began a sect, could quench the zeal of all other believers, and make converts of anyone she merely bid follow.
PAULINA. What! Not women?
SERVANT. Women will love her because she is a woman worth more than any man. Men will love her because she is the rarest of all women.
LEONTES. Go, Cleomenes. Yourself, with your honored friends, bring them to our embrace.
[Exeunt Cleomenes and others.]
Still, it's strange that he should steal upon us like this.
PAULINA. Had our prince, the jewel of children, lived to see this hour, he would have matched well with this lord. There was not quite a month between their births.
LEONTES. Please, no more. Stop. You know he dies to me again when he is talked of. Surely, when I see this gentleman, your words will bring me to think of what may rob me of my reason. They are here.
[Enter Florizel, Perdita, Cleomenes and others.]

Your mother was most true to her marriage, prince, for she printed your royal father off when she conceived you. If I were only twenty-one, your father's image is so struck in you, his very air, that I would call you brother, as I did him, and speak of some wild thing we did before. Most dearly welcome! And your fair princess, a goddess! Oh, alas! I lost a pair who, between heaven and earth, might have stood as you, gracious couple, do now, creating wonder! And then I lost (all through my own folly) the company, and the friendship too, of your brave father, whom, though I bear misery, I wish to live to look on once more.

FLORIZEL. By his command I have landed here in Sicilia, and from him I give you all the greetings a king, as a friend, can send his brother. And if the weakness that waits on worn-out years had not seized his wished-for strength, he would himself have measured out the lands and waters between your throne and his, to look on you, whom he loves (he bade me say so) more than all the scepters and those who bear them alive.

LEONTES. Oh my brother, good gentleman! The wrongs I have done you stir afresh within me. And these kindnesses of yours, so rare, are like interpreters of my own slackness in the past! Welcome here, as spring is to the earth. And has he also exposed this paragon to the fearful and, to say the least, ungentle treatment of dreadful Neptune, to greet a man not worth her trouble, much less the risk of her person?
FLORIZEL. Good my lord, she came from Libya.
LEONTES. Where the warlike Smalus, that noble honored lord, is feared and loved?

FLORIZEL. Most royal sir, from there. From him, whose daughter his tears proclaimed her to be, when he parted from her. From there, with a friendly south wind, we have crossed, to carry out the charge my father gave me, to visit your highness. My best retinue I have dismissed from your Sicilian shores. They are bound for Bohemia, to report not only my success in Libya, sir, but my safe arrival, and my wife's, here where we are.

LEONTES. May the blessed gods purge all infection from our air while you live in this climate! You have a holy father, a gracious gentleman, against whose person, sacred as it is, I have sinned. For that sin the heavens, taking angry note, have left me without children. And your father is blessed, as he deserves from heaven, with you, who are worthy of his goodness. What might I have been, if I could now have looked on a son and daughter, such goodly things as you!
[Enter a Lord.]

LORD. Most noble sir, what I shall report will win no belief, were the proof not so near. Please you, great sir, Bohemia greets you from himself by me. He asks you to arrest his son, who has cast off his dignity and duty both, and fled from his father, from his hopes, and with a shepherd's daughter.
LEONTES. Where is Bohemia? Speak.

LORD. Here in your city. I have just come from him. I speak in amazement, and it suits my wonder and my message. While he was hurrying to your court, in pursuit, it seems, of this fair couple, he meets on the way the father of this seeming lady and her brother, who have both left their country with this young prince.
FLORIZEL. Camillo has betrayed me, whose honor and honesty until now have endured all weathers.
LORD. Lay that to his charge. He is with the king your father.
LEONTES. Who? Camillo?

LORD. Camillo, sir. I spoke with him, and he is now questioning these poor men. I never saw wretches shake so. They kneel, they kiss the earth, and they swear falsely as often as they speak. Bohemia stops his ears and threatens them with various deaths within death.
PERDITA. Oh my poor father! Heaven sets spies on us, and will not have our contract celebrated.
LEONTES. Are you married?
FLORIZEL. We are not, sir, nor are we likely to be. The stars, I see, will kiss the valleys first. The odds for high and low are alike.
LEONTES. My lord, is this the daughter of a king?
FLORIZEL. She is, once she is my wife.

LEONTES. That "once," I see by your good father's speed, will come very slowly. I am sorry, most sorry, that you have broken from his liking, where you were bound in duty. And I am as sorry that your choice is not as rich in worth as in beauty, so that you might well enjoy her.

FLORIZEL. Dear, look up. Though Fortune, visibly an enemy, should chase us with my father, she has no power at all to change our loves. I beg you, sir, remember when you owed no more to time than I do now. With thought of such feelings, step forward as my advocate. At your request my father will grant precious things as trifles.
LEONTES. Would he do so, I'd beg your precious mistress, which he counts as a trifle.
PAULINA. Sir, my liege, your eye has too much youth in it. Not a month before your queen died, she was worth such gazes more than what you look on now.

LEONTES. I was thinking of her even in these looks I made. [_To Florizel._] But your petition is still unanswered. I will go to your father. As long as your honor is not overthrown by your desires, I am a friend to them and to you. On that errand I now go toward him. So follow me, and watch what way I make. Come, good my lord.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — The same. Before the Palace
paragraphs: [Enter Autolycus and a Gentleman.]
AUTOLYCUS. Please, sir, were you there when this story was told?

FIRST GENTLEMAN. I was there when the bundle was opened. I heard the old shepherd tell how he found it. After a moment of amazement, we were all ordered out of the room. All I know is that I thought I heard the shepherd say he found the child.
AUTOLYCUS. I would be very glad to know how it turned out.

FIRST GENTLEMAN. I can only give you a broken account of it. But the changes I saw in the king and Camillo were plain signs of astonishment. They stared at each other so hard they seemed ready to burst their eyes out of their sockets. There was speech in their silence and language in their very gestures. They looked as if they had heard of a world saved, or a world destroyed. They showed a great passion of wonder. But the wisest onlooker, knowing nothing more than what he could see, could not have said whether the news was joy or sorrow. It had to be one of them in the extreme. Here comes a gentleman who may know more.
[Enter a Gentleman.]
What's the news, Rogero?

SECOND GENTLEMAN. Nothing but bonfires. The oracle is fulfilled: the king's daughter is found. Such a wonder has broken out within this hour that ballad-makers could not begin to describe it. Here comes Lady Paulina's steward. He can tell you more.
[Enter a third Gentleman.]
How is it now, sir? This news, which people call true, is so like an old tale that I strongly suspect it isn't. Has the king found his heir?

THIRD GENTLEMAN. It's most true, if truth was ever backed by evidence. What you hear, you'll swear you see, so well do the proofs fit together. There is Queen Hermione's mantle, with her jewel around the baby's neck. There are the letters of Antigonus found with it, which they recognize as his handwriting. There is the majesty of the girl, so like her mother, and the nobility that nature shows in her, above her upbringing. These and many other proofs declare with complete certainty that she is the king's daughter. Did you see the meeting of the two kings?
SECOND GENTLEMAN. No.

THIRD GENTLEMAN. Then you missed a sight that had to be seen and can't be told. You could have watched one joy crown another, in such a way that sorrow seemed to weep as it took its leave, because their joy waded in tears. There was raising of eyes and lifting of hands, and faces so distraught that you could tell them apart only by their clothes, not their features. Our king, ready to leap out of himself for joy at his found daughter, as if that joy had now turned into a loss, cries "Oh, your mother, your mother!" Then he asks Bohemia's forgiveness. Then he embraces his son-in-law. Then he nearly crushes his daughter with hugging her. Now he thanks the old shepherd, who stands by like a weather-beaten fountain statue that has seen many kings' reigns. I never heard of such a meeting. It leaves any report limping behind it and defeats any description.
SECOND GENTLEMAN. What, please tell me, became of Antigonus, who carried the child away?

THIRD GENTLEMAN. Like an old tale again, which will have plenty to tell, though belief is asleep and no ear is open. He was torn to pieces by a bear. The shepherd's son says so, and he has not only his innocence to vouch for him, which counts for a lot, but a handkerchief and rings of Antigonus's that Paulina recognizes.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. What became of his ship and his men?

THIRD GENTLEMAN. Wrecked at the same moment their master died, and in the shepherd's sight. So all the means that helped to abandon the child were lost just when she was found. But oh, the noble battle between joy and sorrow that was fought in Paulina! One eye was cast down for the loss of her husband, the other raised because the oracle was fulfilled. She lifted the princess from the ground, and she locks her in her arms so tightly, as if she would pin her to her heart, so that she could never again be in danger of losing her.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. The dignity of that act was worth an audience of kings and princes, for kings and princes were the ones who acted it.

THIRD GENTLEMAN. One of the prettiest touches of all, the one that fished for my tears (it caught the water, though not the fish), was this. The king told of the queen's death, and how she came to it, bravely confessed and mourned by him. As the princess listened, the story wounded her. From one sign of grief to another, she finally said "Alas," and I would almost say she bled tears, for I am sure my heart wept blood. Whoever was most like marble there changed color. Some fainted, and all sorrowed. If the whole world could have seen it, the grief would have been universal.
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Have they gone back to the court?

THIRD GENTLEMAN. No. The princess heard of her mother's statue, which Paulina keeps. It was many years in the making and has just been finished by that rare Italian master, Julio Romano. If he had eternity himself and could put breath into his work, he would cheat Nature of her trade, so perfectly does he imitate her. He has made Hermione so like Hermione that they say you would speak to her and wait for an answer. They have gone there with all the eagerness of love, and they plan to have supper there.

SECOND GENTLEMAN. I thought she had something important going on there. Ever since Hermione's death she has visited that remote house privately two or three times a day. Shall we go there and add our company to the rejoicing?
FIRST GENTLEMAN. Who would stay away when he has the chance to go in? With every blink of an eye some new wonder will be born. Our absence would make us wasteful of what we could learn. Let's go.
[Exeunt Gentlemen.]

AUTOLYCUS. Now, if I didn't still have a dash of my old life in me, good fortune would drop on my head. I took the old man and his son aboard the prince's ship. I told the prince I'd heard them talking of a bundle and I don't know what. But he was then too fond of the shepherd's daughter (as he took her to be), who was getting very seasick, and he was not much better himself, and the bad weather went on. So the mystery stayed undiscovered. But it's all the same to me. If I had been the one to find out this secret, it would not have tasted right beside my other disgraces.
[Enter Shepherd and Clown.]
Here come the ones I have done good to against my will, already showing in the blossoms of their fortune.
SHEPHERD. Come, boy. I'm past having more children, but your sons and daughters will all be gentlemen born.

CLOWN. Well met, sir. You refused to fight with me the other day because I was no gentleman born. Do you see these clothes? Say you don't see them, and think me still no gentleman born. You'd better say these robes are not gentlemen born. Call me a liar, go on, and see whether I'm not now a gentleman born.
AUTOLYCUS. I know you are now a gentleman born, sir.
CLOWN. Yes, and I have been one for four hours now.
SHEPHERD. And so have I, boy!

CLOWN. So you have. But I was a gentleman born before my father. The king's son took me by the hand and called me brother. Then the two kings called my father brother. Then the prince, my brother, and the princess, my sister, called my father father. And so we wept, and those were the first gentleman-like tears we ever shed.
SHEPHERD. We may live, son, to shed many more.
CLOWN. Yes, or else it would be hard luck, being in such a topsy-turvy position as we are.
AUTOLYCUS. I humbly beg you, sir, to pardon all the faults I have committed against your worship, and to speak well of me to the prince my master.
SHEPHERD. Please, son, do it. We must be gentle now that we are gentlemen.
CLOWN. Will you mend your ways?
AUTOLYCUS. Yes, if it please your good worship.
CLOWN. Give me your hand. I will swear to the prince that you are as honest and true a fellow as any in Bohemia.
SHEPHERD. You may say it, but not swear it.
CLOWN. Not swear it, now that I'm a gentleman? Let peasants and yeomen say it. I'll swear it.
SHEPHERD. What if it's false, son?

CLOWN. However false it is, a true gentleman may swear it on behalf of his friend. And I'll swear to the prince that you are a brave fighter and that you won't get drunk. But I know you are no brave fighter and that you will get drunk. Still, I'll swear it, and I wish you would be a brave fighter.
AUTOLYCUS. I'll prove to be one, sir, as best I can.

CLOWN. Yes, by all means prove a brave fighter. If I don't wonder how you dare get drunk when you're not a brave fighter, never trust me. Listen! The kings and the princes, our relatives, are going to see the queen's picture. Come, follow us. We'll be your good masters.
[Exeunt.]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 3 — The same. A Room in Paulina’s house
paragraphs: [Enter Leontes, Polixenes, Florizel, Perdita, Camillo, Paulina, Lords and Attendants.]
LEONTES. Oh, good and serious Paulina, what great comfort you have given me!

PAULINA. Sovereign sir, if I did not do well, I meant well. You have paid back all my services in full. But that you have granted my poor house a visit, together with your fellow king and these heirs of your kingdoms who are now engaged, is a surplus of your favor. I could not live long enough to repay it.

LEONTES. Oh, Paulina, we honor you with trouble. But we came to see the statue of our queen. We have passed through your gallery, and we were very pleased with many of its rare pieces. But we did not see what my daughter came to look at, the statue of her mother.

PAULINA. As she was peerless in life, so her dead likeness, I truly believe, surpasses anything you have looked at or any human hand has made. That is why I keep it alone, apart. But here it is. Get ready to see life imitated as closely as sleep ever imitated death. Look, and say it is well done.
[Paulina draws back a curtain, and reveals Hermione standing as a statue.]
I like your silence. It shows your wonder all the better. But still, speak. First you, my lord. Doesn't it come somewhere near her?

LEONTES. Her natural posture! Scold me, dear stone, so that I can truly say you are Hermione. Or rather, you are she in your not scolding, for she was as gentle as infancy and grace. But Paulina, Hermione was not so wrinkled, not nearly so old as this looks.
POLIXENES. Oh, not by much!
PAULINA. All the more credit to our carver's skill, which skips some sixteen years and makes her look as she would now.

LEONTES. As she might have looked now. It comforts me as much as it now pierces my soul. Oh, this is how she stood, with just such majestic life, warm life, as she now stands coldly, when I first courted her! I am ashamed. Doesn't the stone rebuke me for being more stone than it is? Oh, royal work, there is magic in your majesty. It has called my wrongs back to my memory, and it has taken the spirit out of your admiring daughter, who stands like stone beside you.
PERDITA. Allow me, and do not call it superstition, to kneel and ask for her blessing. Lady, dear queen, who ended when I had only begun, give me your hand to kiss.
PAULINA. Oh, patience! The statue has only just been finished. The paint is not dry.

CAMILLO. My lord, your sorrow was laid on too heavily. Sixteen winters cannot blow it away, nor sixteen summers dry it up. Hardly any joy ever lived so long, and no sorrow but killed itself much sooner.
POLIXENES. Dear brother, let the man who caused this have the power to take away as much of your grief as he can make up in himself.
PAULINA. Indeed, my lord, if I had thought the sight of my poor image would affect you like this (for the stone is mine), I would not have shown it.
LEONTES. Do not draw the curtain.
PAULINA. You must not gaze at it any longer, or your imagination may soon think it moves.
LEONTES. Leave it, leave it. I wish I were dead, except that already I think — Who was it that made it? See, my lord, wouldn't you think it breathed? And that those veins truly carried blood?
POLIXENES. Masterfully done. The very life seems warm upon her lip.
LEONTES. There is movement in the fixed look of her eye, as if art were mocking us.
PAULINA. I'll draw the curtain. My lord is almost so carried away that he will soon think it lives.
LEONTES. Oh, sweet Paulina, make me think so for twenty years together! No sound senses in the world can match the pleasure of that madness. Leave it alone.
PAULINA. I am sorry, sir, that I have stirred you this far. But I could upset you further.

LEONTES. Do, Paulina, for this upset has a taste as sweet as any soothing cordial. I still think there is a breath coming from her. What fine chisel could ever carve breath? Let no man mock me, for I will kiss her!
PAULINA. Good my lord, hold back. The red on her lip is wet. You'll spoil it if you kiss it, and stain your own lips with oily paint. Shall I draw the curtain?
LEONTES. No, not for twenty years.
PERDITA. I could stand here that long, looking on.

PAULINA. Either hold back and leave the chapel at once, or prepare for more amazement. If you can bear to watch, I'll make the statue truly move, come down, and take you by the hand. But then you'll think (which I protest against) that I am helped by wicked powers.
LEONTES. Whatever you can make her do, I am content to watch. Whatever you can make her say, I am content to hear. It is as easy to make her speak as to make her move.
PAULINA. You must awaken your faith. Then everyone stand still. Or let those who think what I am doing is unlawful go away.
LEONTES. Go on. No foot will stir.

PAULINA. Music, awake her: play! [_Music._] It's time. Come down. Be stone no more. Come closer. Strike with wonder everyone who looks on. Come, I'll fill your grave up. Move, no, come away. Leave your numbness to death, for dear life redeems you from him. You see she stirs.
[Hermione comes down from the pedestal.]

Don't be afraid. Her actions will be holy, as you hear that my spell is lawful. Do not shun her until you see her die again, for then you kill her twice. No, offer your hand. When she was young you courted her. Now that she is old, has she become the suitor?
LEONTES.
[_Embracing her._] Oh, she's warm!
If this is magic, let it be an art as lawful as eating.
POLIXENES. She embraces him.
CAMILLO. She hangs about his neck. If she belongs to life, let her speak too.
POLIXENES. Yes, and let her make clear where she has lived, or how she was stolen from the dead.

PAULINA. If you were only told that she is living, you would hoot at it like an old tale. But it appears she lives, though she does not speak yet. Watch a little while. If you please, step in, fair madam. Kneel and ask your mother's blessing. Turn, good lady. Our Perdita is found.
[Presenting Perdita who kneels to Hermione.]

HERMIONE. You gods, look down, and from your sacred vials pour your graces on my daughter's head! Tell me, my own child, where have you been kept safe? Where did you live? How did you find your father's court? For you shall hear that I, knowing from Paulina that the oracle gave hope you were alive, have kept myself alive to see how it ends.

PAULINA. There's time enough for that, in case they want, at this moment, to trouble your joys with a similar story. Go together, you precious winners all. Share your joy with everyone. As for me, an old turtledove, I will fly to some withered branch and there mourn my mate, who is never to be found again, until I am lost.

LEONTES. Oh, peace, Paulina! You should take a husband with my consent, as I took a wife with yours. This is a match, made between us by vows. You have found my wife, though how is still to be questioned, for I saw her, as I thought, dead, and said many a prayer in vain over her grave. I won't have to look far (for him, I partly know his mind) to find you an honorable husband. Come, Camillo, and take her by the hand. Her worth and honesty are richly noted, and here proved by us, a pair of kings. Let's go from this place. What! Look at my brother. I ask both your pardons, that I ever put my ill suspicion between your holy looks. This is your son-in-law, the son of the king, who by the heavens' direction is betrothed to your daughter. Good Paulina, lead us from here, where we may at leisure each ask and answer about his part in this wide gap of time since we were first separated. Quickly, lead on!
[Exeunt.]
